Without explicit constraints, even minor control adjustments can lead to unintended control loop closures, complicating optimization and stability analysis. To address this, a novel task called Simultaneous Robotic Structure (SRS) Service has been developed to maintain the system's underlying structure throughout control applications. By reinterpreting the problem as a control service, searching for robust solutions becomes necessary, and we introduce a new service framework to provide such solutions. To demonstrate the effectiveness of SRS Service, we show that the Simultaneous Robotic Structure (SRS) Service Problem with Sample Path Convenience is computationally solvable in two different scenarios: one with a mechanical formulation and another with an augmented Lagrangian method. Additionally, we provide a relaxation to show that a near-optimal solution with performance close to that of a sample path optimal solution can be achieved through a convex program. To address the noise and disturbances that commonly affect robotic control systems, we develop a robust control algorithm by reinterpreting the problem as a Simultaneous Robotic Structure (SRS) Service Problem with Uncertainties. Lastly, we verify the computational power of SRS Service through simulation-based evaluation and demonstrate its practical applicability to actual robotic control systems. To the best of our knowledge, SRS Service presents a novel and groundbreaking approach to maintaining the system's underlying structure in robotic control systems. Deep learning pre-training for semantic segmentation has become a widely accepted practice. It's common for segmentation models to be pre-trained using tasks like image classification, but recent advances in monocular depth estimation have led some to suggest this alternative pre-training method to create segmentation models that better generalise. We investigated whether monocular depth estimation pre-training is indeed superior to classification-based pre-training by exploring its potential to aid validation set object detection during testing. We discovered that while it offers some improvement, it doesn't provide significant benefits. We also observed that models trained on the ADE20K dataset using monocular depth estimation and image classification objectives performed better on novel objects than those trained only on classification tasks. However, rather than recommending a change to classification-based pre-training, we suggest customizing the choice of pre-training task and object class for specific datasets to enhance performance. The findings are supported by experiments conducted across multiple tasks and datasets. The code and dataset are available on GitHub. For instance, our results show that models pre-trained on the ADE20K dataset to predict the 'tree' class through monomatic depth estimation are able to correctly classify 34% more trees on SUN360 than models pre-trained through classification. Similarly, our findings show that models pre-trained on the PASCAL VOC dataset using monomatic depth estimation to predict the 'car' class are able to correctly identify 21% more cars in SUN360 than models pre-trained through classification. These results suggest that while monomatic depth estimation pre-training may provide some benefits, it is not a significantly superior method of pre-training for semantic segmentation. We also discovered that for specific datasets and object classes, customising the choice of pre-training task can lead to better results. For example, our results show that for the 'tree' class in ADE20K, monomatic depth estimation pre-training is not as effective as classification pre-training, but for the 'car' class in PASCAL VOC, it is more effective. This suggests that while we do not recommend changing the standard classification-based pre-training for semantic segmentation, we do recommend customising the choice of pre-training method and object class for different tasks. Ultimately, our results show that semantic segmentation models pre-trained using various methods perform well on novel objects, but there is still room for improvement in object identification within scenes. For instance, our results show that while our top-performing models are able to correctly classify over 80% of objects in the test set, they are still struggling with object detection within scenes. In this context, we explore NK1 groups, specifically in the context of graded rings and hypergroups. Bak introduced NK1 groups in relation to graded groups, explaining that any graded group derived from a crossed product of a group and a graded module is an NK1 group. Our study reveals that only finite NK1 groups over graded rings with a unity are Hopf groups. When the graded ring lacks a unity, we identify the condition under which a unity can be implanted on the graded ring, thus allowing us to determine the NK1 groups that can be unified. Additionally, we demonstrate that NK1 groups over Hopf groups with a coassociative coproduct are Hopf groups, provided that the graded ring's unity does not conflict with the Hopf group's unity. Related results concerning collectivist groups, Hopf groups, and hypergroups are also presented. An investigation into NK1 groups over commutative Hopf groups with a finite order reveals that only groups such as the 2-group, tor, and affine groups can be NK1 groups, except when the graded ring's unity does not match the Hopf group's unity, in which case any collectivist group over the implanted ring can be NK1. Finally, we show that NK1 groups over implanted rings can be Hopf groups, but only in cases where the implanted and original unities are the same. Related results concerning group-graded Hopf algebras are also presented. Our study concludes by identifying and describing specific NK1 groups over implanted rings, such as NK1 groups over implanted rings implanted again, collectivist groups over implanted rings implanted by Z2, and Hopf groups over implanted rings implanted again, particularly group-graded Hopf algebras. Finally, we illustrate with an example why only finite Hopf groups can be NK1 groups over graded rings with a unity. This example demonstrates that an infinite Hopf group, such as the free Hopf group on R, cannot be NK1 over a graded ring such as R[t]. Moreover, we reveal that a unity can be implanted on the graded ring NK1(R, R[t]) only to fail, thus precluding the possibility of a unity being implanted on the graded ring R[t] to make NK1(R, R[t]) a Hopf group. Evolutionary algorithms are commonly used for solving complex multi-objective optimization problems, and they often benefit from running in parallel, but may experience delays due to a phenomenon known as evaluation time bias. This occurs because the algorithm invests more time in individuals with better qualities, and less time in those waiting for their evaluation. Parent selection is typically used in multi-objective evolution strategies to ensure diversity by selecting parents based on a population ranking. A new parent selection approach, the frequency-based parent selection, aims to reduce evaluation time bias by considering how often an individual has been selected in addition to its ranking. In this paper, we evaluate the effectiveness of the frequency-based parent selection and propose an alternative, the frequency-centered parent selection, to improve results by forgetting rankings over time and preserving them for better diversity. Experimental results show that the frequency-centered parent selection achieves better results than the original frequency-based parent selection and surpasses the multi-objective Pareto Genetic Algorithm in solving a complex optimization problem using asynchronous computing. Parent selection performance is also compared when using a population ranking versus an instantaneous ranking. In addition, a new method is proposed to balance the gap between the best and worst results, known as gap balancing, which can be used independently of parent selection. Parent selection methods exhibit a significant improvement over a leading asynchronous computational method on a complex optimization problem that features a large number of dimensions, constraints, and objectives. In particular, the frequency-centered parent selection achieves a higher quality, greater diversity, and faster convergence of non-dominated solutions. A major factor contributing to its success is its ability to preserve rankings over time, which has a positive impact on results. Moreover, the frequency-centered parent selection does not require any problem-specific information and is easy to implement. A major drawback of the frequency-centered parent selection is its reduced ability to select the best individuals, which in turn may lead to a lower solution quality compared to parent selection methods that do not forget rankings. Nonetheless, the frequency-centered parent selection demonstrates a substantial potential for use in a wide range of multi-objective optimization problems. In particular, the method can be easily integrated into the SP-MOGO framework, which is a general computational framework for addressing various multi-objective optimization challenges. A major challenge remains to be automating the selection of suitable parameters for the frequency-centered parent selection. In addition, future work may involve the extension of this approach to evolutionary algorithms that rely on a continuous ranking. In linguistically diverse societies, where people often switch between multiple languages, the prevalence of language play is significant. We examine a labeling game scenario where players can use multiple languages and participate in it as a form of voluntary work. The game's setup encourages players to adopt a uniform 'lexicon' for work purposes, but there's no mechanism ensuring they stick to it. As part of our study on this game, we investigated how the size of the active player population, or community, affects the emergence of a consistent language pattern over time. We discovered that smaller player populations tend to achieve consistency faster, achieving it more often, although consistency levels themselves do not necessarily improve with population size. Additionally, we observed that communities where players are allowed to move between groups, or 'diasporas,' achieve consistency at approximately the same rate as larger player populations, indicating that diaspora structure can contribute to the emergence of consistent languages at a population-dependent level. Finally, we identified 'critical sizes' for both the player population and diaspora structures that increase the likelihood of consistency across all community configurations. The findings from our studies, using both comprehensive simulations and a specific game scenario, reveal the complex interplay between voluntary work and the emergence of consistent languages as a collaborative endeavor. The results can inform how to design, rather than prevent, language diversity, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation across multiple language speakers. However, when these networks are confronted with equations containing multiple variables and high-order derivatives, they can experience significant challenges due to a phenomenon called spectral bias. This issue causes certain momentum-based optimization methods to consistently converge towards solutions that favor low-frequency components, thus neglecting crucial high-frequency details. We have found that using stochastic gradient descent with momentum is less susceptible to this spectral bias problem compared to other optimization techniques. We have also developed a novel method to tackle spectral bias by incorporating high-frequency components as necessary conditions for the optimization process. This method views these conditions as additional constraints for the optimization problem, thereby informing the design of PINN layers. We have tested various PINN architectures, including layers with global attention that can sample and aggregate details from the boundary conditions, as well as layers with local attention that can accurately apply boundary conditions. We have also employed a combination of these optimized layers to develop a universal multi-scale neural operator that can effectively solve multi-scale PDE systems. We have demonstrated the capabilities of this operator by solving the multi-phase Navier-Stokes equations for the two-dimensional slug flow benchmark at high Reynolds numbers. The proposed method has the potential to expand the applications of PINNs for multi-scale PDE systems, thus extending their possible uses to systems with even higher Reynolds numbers. A transparent Black Box solution to reinforcement learning is developed, combining inductive logic programming with deep reinforcement learning techniques using Q-values. This involves integrating a public Q-value function as a layer within the model, which can be accessed by an external ILP reasoner providing explanations at the state-action level. These explanations, generated through ILP's induction process, can identify actions associated with achieved goals, enabling zero-shot learning by discovering novel action-goal pairs in unsupervised scenarios. Moreover, the system's ability to extract general action-taking strategies allows it to adapt to novel multi-action, multi-goal domains without the need for explicit reward functions. Through experimental evaluation on various scenarios with increased complexity, the proposed approach demonstrates its ability to learn and generalize in settings where policy evaluation relies on a reasoner's efficiency. Additionally, the ILP reasoner's limitations are utilized to demonstrate the availability of actionable explanations from deep reinforcement learning systems. Overall, the proposed method overcomes the main limitation associated with explaining black box models and facilitates transparent learning at intermediate representation levels. The aim is to automate verification for a broader range of programs, including safety-critical ones. The innovative concept of Natural Hoare Reasoning seamlessly links together natural language descriptions used in writing programs and the formal specifications to validate them through Hoare logic. This new approach is an advanced and efficient variation of Hoare logic that accurately translates logical forms into programs and utilizes domain knowledge.
 
 This paper outlines a novel framework, Natural Hoare Reasoning, that effectively links natural language descriptions with Hoare logic, enabling the automatic translation of formal specifications into programs. The advancements in this work include a new reasoning rule and a developed algorithm that automatically verify a significant portion of imperative programs with the assistance of a parser that accurately translates logical forms into programs.
 
 The evaluation of the proposed method demonstrates its capacity to automatically validate programs from logical forms in approximately 40ms for a substantial dataset of 1052 program verifications across various domains, including data and control flow.
 
 The potential applications of this technique are vast, including the automatic validation of programs generated by NL-based compilers as part of a compiler pipeline, and offering a formal guarantee for safety-critical programs, among others. A localized enhancement of these particles, or 'events,' has been observed near the moon's orbit and attributed to a shock wave's impact on the solar magnetic field. Although the effect is most pronounced near the moon, similar events have been observed on spacecraft in interplanetary space and at Earth, suggesting a global phenomenon. In this study, we adapt this model to analyze data from the RETel particle detector on the Challenger satellite and compare its results to actual data, with a focus on detecting events captured at low Earth orbit. We also discuss the underlying physics of these events and their potential to answer outstanding questions in particle astrophysics.

Recent observations of CIDA1, a heavily rotating T-type star, have revealed signs of a massive planet in the early stages of formation. Data from SPHERE/Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur's SARTHA project indicate that the planet, referred to as CIDA-6b, has a mass of around $10\,M_J$ and an orbital period of $230\,days$. This young planet is thought to be responsible for the star's orbital eccentricity and its effects on the surrounding disk. Using ALMA, the team observed CIDA1's disk and found evidence of a massive, off-center ring. This unique morphology can be explained by a massive planet inducing a bar-like feature and a shock wave that formed a cap-like structure in the disk's gas surface density. Modeling this phenomenon using thermo-dynamic equations and a shearing box method confirms that the system is dominated by the planet's influence. These observations of CIDA1's disk provide the first visual signs of planet-disk interactions in extremely low-mass stars, and have significant implications for understanding the early formation of planets in these systems. CIDA1's disk is estimated to be around $70\,au$ in radius, and its orbital eccentricity around $0.5$, and further formation is expected to be seen over the next few years. This study has provided the first images of accreting protoplanets in very low-mass stars and demonstrates the importance of SPHERE's second generation instruments in observing the formation of planets beyond Saturn's orbit. CIDA1's system serves as a prime target for future instruments such as ALMA's, JWST's and ELT's facilities and highlights its potential to reveal the earliest stages of planetary formation in very low-mass stars. Static analysis through abstract interpretation offers a way to make precise predictions about program behavior without running them. It does this by simulating a program's behavior with an abstract representation, but this simulation often overestimates program behavior. This limitation causes analysis tools to be too cautious, which is particularly problematic for programs with declining phases. In such cases, early warnings are given even if, in reality, problems occur much later. We present a novel technique to differentiate between a program's ascent and descent by incorporating a new abstract domain. This representation, made of a limited set of markers, follows a program's state and triggers specialization only when it indicates a program peak. An operational way to manage these markers is proposed along with a protocol to maintain precision. The technique is successfully applied to a few algorithms, demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving better trade-offs between soundness and caution. Evaluation shows that, with the new decoupling analysis, soundness is reached much faster than with traditional single-phase approaches, with a notable improvement for programs with a pronounced decline. Moreover, this contribution is compatible with existing abstract domains, allowing it to be easily integrated into existing sound analysis tools. In particular, it is shown that it can be integrated with the widely used three-valued logic without compromising soundness. Finally, decoupling analysis is also useful as a middle phase between sound ascent analyses and cautious descent analyses. Experiments confirm its effectiveness in reducing overestimation when used as a middle phase. Moreover, decoupling analysis is shown to be applicable to other existing sound analysis techniques, opening up possibilities for their improvement. An implementation of the presented techniques is available at https://bitbucket.org/fgisdecoupling/fgis-aa/. It integrates with the Astro development tools at https://astro-dev.github.io/. Astro's tools already include a generic representation of the decoupling abstract domain, as well as an integration of the presented specialization technique. This integration with Astro's tools is intended to promote the presented techniques to a widely available analysis tool. An explanation of Astro's concepts and decoupling integration can be found in the related note https://bitbucket.org/fgisdecoupling/fgis-aa/#markdown-headerrelated-work. These phonons have a long lifetime and can store significant amounts of energy. When excited, these phonons can achieve remarkably high energies of 1 eV, corresponding to a wavelength of 1250 nm at room temperature. To demonstrate this, we use quantum atomic simulations to investigate the phonon mode in oxygen-doped manganite and hole-doped titanate perovskites. In our research, we address the problem of identifying anomalies in multi-dimensional spaces efficiently and with high precision. Our novel technique is implemented as a Java library, available for immediate use. This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and develops approximative solutions using an iterative approach. First, we derive solutions based on Michaelis-Menten kinetics and reveal that they align with existing iterative models in the literature. Subsequently, we derive solutions for reversible enzyme reactions incorporating inhibition, which are also applicable in single-turnover experiments. To this end, we present a mathematical framework combining power series and perturbation theory. Our analysis shows that iterative models can be used as approximative solutions for enzyme reactions, even in situations where steady-state conditions are not satisfied. Moreover, we highlight the necessity of considering enzyme and substrate/substrate analogue states in perturbation theory. To validate our analytical solutions, we perform numerical simulations, which demonstrate that the iterative models can accurately describe experimental data, particularly at low substrate analogue concentrations and under steady-state conditions. However, we observe larger deviations for high substrate analogue concentrations. Finally, we discuss the limitations and potential pitfalls of iterative models in kinetic modeling. This knowledge can be valuable in the development of mathematical models for enzyme kinetics and pharmacokinetics. Additionally, we provide practical guidance on how to implement the analytical solutions in real-world scenarios. Although the solutions are analytical, we perform numerical computations due to the inevitable presence of round-off errors. We utilize examples from the fields of biochemical kinetics and pharmacokinetics to illustrate our approach. Moreover, we present a comprehensive Python package that can be used to perform similar computations in these domains. This package is compatible with both Python 2 and 3 and can be easily installed via a pip command. We also address common pitfalls in the solutions for kinetic models and pharmacokinetic modeling. Related work is also discussed in the context of the provided solutions. This includes the derivation of power series and perturbation theory, as well as the development of iterative models and their connection to existing Michaelis-Menten kinetics and steady-state analyses. Ultimately, we perform a thorough error analysis to determine the applicability of the iterative models in kinetic modeling and pharmacokinetic modeling. This error analysis reveals that the iterative models are generally accurate, except in situations where substrate analogue concentrations are very high. This is particularly the case in single-turnover experiments and inhibition kinetics. Nonetheless, we anticipate that the iterative models remain a valuable tool in these situations as an approximative solution. We introduce a set of stochastic expectation swells defined by the stochastic terminal condition $\mathcal{E}[\tau-\tau_0]_{t|T}= -\int_{t
  \tau_0} \tau \mathcal{E}[\tau_0|P] d\tau$. These financial swells are analyzed in terms of their mathematical properties, including Hessian and quadratic approximation, with a special focus on their application to stochastic terminal conditions in mathematical finance. Furthermore, we discuss a novel method for detecting arbitrage opportunities in financial markets, which are characterized by Stochastic Mean-Reverting Termination Durations. This arbitrage detection method relies on a dimension reduction technique and is tested on simulated financial swells with varying parameters. We also investigate the connection between our swells and well-known financial equations such as the Black-Scholes and Amini-Mazrogiou models. This enables us to derive diagnostic equations for these well-established models by employing our stochastic terminal condition approach. Moreover, we establish a general strategy for representing financial swells as sums of pure states and mixed states, which in turn allows us to derive diagnostic equations for a broad range of financial phenomena, including mean-reverting behavior. This analytical framework serves as the basis for our numerical methods in mathematical finance. Finally, we outline a strategy for using our analytical framework to diagnose a spectrum of financial phenomena, from stochastic volatility to arbitrage opportunities. The analytical framework presented here is versatile and can be applied to a diverse set of stochastic terminal conditions, including those featuring Gaussian, Exponential, Power, and Logarithmic distributions. Furthermore, we have successfully tested our dimension reduction technique and diagnostic equations on simulated financial swells with varying parameters. This research has also inspired a novel method for detecting and preventing phishing attacks on financial swells with a unique termination condition. Recent advances in personalized recommendation have led to significant improvements in practical solutions. Research has shown that users' reviews and ratings contain valuable information for understanding item features and making high-quality recommendations. To address this, we develop a unique task - evaluation-based item recommendation, which utilizes ratings and reviews to infer recommended items that users would want to evaluate. To solve this, we propose the Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), which models interactions between users', items', and reviewers' features and combines them with sentiment-aware review analysis. Experimental results on two real-world datasets showcase the effectiveness of SIFN in comparative performance. Additionally, we release a dataset with 102K reviews and 1.2 Million sentences to support further research in NLP and recommender systems.

We introduce a novel, non-detection based method for image registration called LoFTR. This approach captures local features with a transformer architecture and generates a high-quality, dense correspondence map from the image features. By leveraging spatially localized image regions in each image, LoFTR circumvents the limitations of traditional methods that were over-reliant on global image features. Furthermore, we showcase the applicability of our method for real-time image registration in applications such as video compression. By analyzing data from NASA's SBSPACE database, researchers created a worldwide blaze prediction model. It was discovered that blaze occurrences exhibit a cyclical pattern tied to the 27-day solar rotation period but are also influenced by intense solar coronal mass ejections, showing a correlation with magnetic field data from the sun. Ultimately, by analyzing CME events and corresponding regional blazes on the solar surface, researchers were able to forecast their future paths and times of arrival on the solar surface. We examine various measures of morphological intricacy within English texts, 
correlating them to expert judgments of text intricacy. We also evaluate the 
efficacy of these measures in authenticating texts based on their intricacy levels.
In this study, we applied several corpora-based metrics of morphological intricacy 
to sets of written texts that differ in their level of intricacy - either 
naturally occurring or artificially constructed. We compared the metrics' 
performance in authenticating the text groups and found that while they all 
correlated with the text categories, the results suggest that only one of these 
metrics, $\mathcal{I}_m$, is capable of distinguishing between the text groups. 
Furthermore, we found that although the metrics correlate with the text categories, 
the results of linear discriminant analysis indicate that only a small subset of 
words is responsible for differentiating the text groups. We also discovered that 
nonspecialist writers tend to produce texts with lower intricacy. However, the 
metrics' performance in authenticating the text groups using random forest classifiers 
was mixed, with only two classifiers - $\mathcal{I}_m$ and $\mathcal{I}_p$ - 
achieving above-chance performance in a ten-fold cross-validation. Ultimately, our 
findings suggest that only $\mathcal{I}_m$ is capable of distinguishing between 
the text groups, with the possibility of further improving its performance by 
introducing additional linguistic features. We also compared the performance of the 
metrics when using a combination of expert and non-expert writers as a reference 
category, with the results indicating that only $\mathcal{I}_m$ achieves significant 
separation of the text groups. Building upon this insight, we propose a model that 
uses a mixture of distributions to model a reference category consisting of both 
expert and non-expert texts, with the results again suggesting that only $\mathcal{I}_m$ achieves significant separation of the text groups. Finally, our paper addresses limitations and raises questions regarding the performance of the metrics, with suggestions for future research outlined in the conclusion. In various complex machine learning models, it can be challenging to determine which components, such as individual neurons in a neural network, contribute significantly to the outcome. To address this issue, researchers have developed techniques to analyze and interpret how neural networks classify input patterns. By utilizing specialized hardware or algorithms that perform symbolic computations, model analysis can provide insight into the complex processes behind a model's predictions. However, these techniques can be applied only after a model has been fully trained and require substantial computational resources. As a result, they are not suitable for large or complex models that may take a long time to train, such as those with billions of parameters, and models where only partial information about pattern classification is available. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a new technique called Insight. It allows analysts to leverage general insights into pattern classification, without knowing the full training data or model architecture. By symbolically executing parts of the model in parallel, Insight identifies which model components contribute to the given classification tasks. Our research demonstrates that the model components identified by Insight are relevant and precise, and the model can be simplified by disabling them to reduce computation. We have evaluated our approach on various datasets, such as MNIST, CIFAR10, and ImageNet, and showed that the model can be modified to achieve the same accuracy while using fewer parameters and reducing inference time by a factor of 1.4. To the best of our knowledge, our technique is a first attempt to apply symbolic model analysis to deep learning models using only partial insights into pattern classification. It is available for public use, and we are now exploring its extension to support performance-based model analysis. It is observed that certain GMSK-based schemes, such as the frequency pulse position modulation (FPPP) and the time pulse position modulation (TPPP), can be viewed as variations of the conventional GMSK detection. This connection enables us to draw some important conclusions regarding these schemes, particularly with regard to their differential detection properties. Specifically, it can be shown that certain GMSK-based codes, including FPPG and TPPG, only offer advantage in terms of improved differential encoding, but do not actually enhance the differential detection process. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that these codes can be modified to improve their performance through specific code transformations. This modification results in improved performance for certain code variants, such as $G_{1/2}$-GMSK, which can outperform the conventional GMSK under certain conditions. Moreover, it is shown that these code variants can be viewed as part of a larger family of continuous phase modulation schemes known as Partial Response Continuous Phase Modulation (PRCPM). This family of GMSK-based codes can be designed to offer improved performance, including enhanced differential performance, by selecting specific code variants, such as $G_{1/3}$-GMSK. rankings among local data clusters and then organizing them in a hierarchical structure
for more efficient search. This can be accomplished by integrating a cluster detection
algorithm or by dividing the dataset manually into groups. In VSC-Rank's implementation,
our primary focus is on the latter option and we demonstrate its effectiveness
using two benchmark datasets: the Cross-Domain Slot Filling Task and the MultiJetCar
dataset. In both cases, VSC-Rank yields better policy results and reduces training time
by nearly 50% compared to the state-of-the-art Transference method. Additionally, we
examine how VSC-Rank's performance compares to other recent transfer reinforcement
learning techniques in scenarios where no domain adaptation is involved. Empirical
results indicate that VSC-Rack's parameters can be determined relatively swiftly,
with most components requiring only a few hours to train, and we provide our code
and configuration files for reproduction purposes. This research was supported by

We investigate the statistical properties of the eigenvalue spectra of altered random band matrices, specifically those modified with finite-rank complex matrices. To broaden our understanding, we also explore the unaltered random band matrices. Both distributions converge to semi-circular and Marchenko-Pastur density measures. Estimations for convergence times and laws of large numbers for related spectral parameters are also developed. This research relies on the advancements made in the statistical physics field, including the semi-circle law and disorder averaging. This approach allows us to obtain a simple, yet effective method for estimating the rank of the modifying matrix, which is based on the expectation of eigenvalue counting functions. This method is then validated through the use of Monte-Carlo simulations. These outcomes reveal that our estimates are consistent across various matrix dimensions and ranks. Moreover, the statistical physics framework enables the recovery of the underlying model through the use of the Wick rotation, which is a non-perturbative approach. However, the application of this method is hindered by the presence of ambiguities in the choice of rotation time. Nonetheless, the combination of our density estimation method and the application of the Wick rotation yields highly accurate results, which are comparable to the outcomes of the Monte-Carlo simulations. This combination of methods is envisioned to be widely applicable for the estimation of statistical characteristics of eigenvalue spectra in the field of statistical physics. Finally, the application of our density estimation method is not limited to the random band matrices, as it can be extended to a broader range of random matrix models, including the Altland-Zirnbauer and Altland-Zirnbauer 9-fold classification. However, the estimation of parameters other than the rank are still pending. This research is expected to contribute to the estimation of eigenvalue spectra in various domains of statistical physics. Anomaly detection under loosely supervised or tiny ML conditions presents significant challenges, particularly in data sets where instances are sparse or scarce. Anomaly detection under such constraints demands efficient and robust algorithms that can operate effectively even with limited data availability. One approach to anomaly detection is isolation, which involves identifying one-off instances. For sparse data sets, high-coverage isolation algorithms are necessary, which can be resource-intensive to train. To address this, the TiWS-iForest algorithm has been developed, offering an out-of-the-box solution for anomaly isolation in loosely supervised and tiny ML environments. TiWS-iForest utilizes weighted instances and random sampling to optimize iForest for tiny data sets, achieving improved robustness and efficiency. Experimental evaluations of TiWS-iForest demonstrate its superiority over other isolation algorithms, showcasing its potential to detect anomalies in data sets where traditional algorithms fail. Furthermore, the code and pre-trained models for TiWS-iForest are openly available on GitHub. Overall, the results highlight the significance of efficient isolation in detecting anomalies under loosely supervised and tiny ML conditions. This interpretation relies on consistent state vectors, $\rho$-states, and Fock states containing the same amount of information before and after measurement. This book provides evidence that this interpretation is not only feasible, but also necessary for making accurate predictions in quantum physics. This evidence is drawn from numerous examples throughout the field, highlighting how quantum coherence is essential for resolving various problems, such as superposition, interference, the given options, spin measurements, the double-slit experiment, the spin-squeezed microscope, and the physics of light interacting with matter. Ultimately, this book argues that quantum coherence plays a critical role in quantum physics and that its loss through decoherence should not be considered an inherent feature of quantum physics. Instead, this book suggests that preserving coherence is always an achievable goal, either by eliminating decoherence or by incorporating it into a larger Coherence-Decoherence-Entanglement (CDE) framework that is based on an extension of the established Particle-Particle (PP) framework in condensed matter theory. This issue has been resolved using a technique known as the best response update process, but learning this approach can be difficult due to its slow convergence and the large memory requirements needed to store the complex matrices necessary for analysis. This ability to learn predictive models of dynamic processes is a major breakthrough in machine learning, and FPNs can be used to simulate various types of best response processes on real-world games, such as the Prisoner's Dilemma. Furthermore, FPNs can be extended to predict equilibrium states in situations where only partial game information is available, and can also be applied to problems outside of game theory and economics. Our approach is grounded in the principle of causality, where we define a causal influence from one event to another as a correlation that consistently predicts the latter. Focusing on Gaussian 1o events, we identify the lower bounds for their mutual information based on a correlation measure. Next, we consider two events, where the cause precedes the effect, and derive a bound for the cause-to-effect mutual information as a function of the effect size. Our results in dimensions 1 and 2 are demonstrated through specific examples, and we show the lower bound for the mutual information in these cases is the smallest it can be. Additionally, we apply our findings to a communication scenario where the source of information is divided between two receivers, and we determine the minimum possible rate at which they can decode messages from a high-dimensional signal, as well as the associated processing delay in such a setting. Our study also considers a signal detection problem, where the task is to identify the orientation of a high-dimensional vector, and we calculate the minimum possible signal duration required for this operation. Finally, we compare our results with the information-theoretic bounds derived by Schr\"oderer and Sutter in higher dimensions, and we note that in these cases the bounds we obtained are higher than the ones presented there. Networked LTI systems are becoming increasingly significant in critical areas, yet they're vulnerable to covert cyber assaults that can go undetected. These assaults can compromise both network and control functions, but the stealth of the attackers makes it hard to spot when and how they occurred. Because there's no explicit information about when and where these assaults may happen, it's challenging to design effective detection methods. This work introduces a new surveillance strategy called effective predictive surveillance (EPS) that focuses on distinguishing between system behavior and malicious activity. EPS is based on a predictive model which utilizes a slip-free attack scenario and a safety margin to separate normal and malicious data. This approach is scalable, model-agnostic, and model-dependent, offering a versatile solution for various situations. Moreover, it's the first method that doesn't need explicit attack models to detect malicious behavior. Experimental outcomes using both simulation and real-world data show the effectiveness of the EPS method in distinguishing between malicious and normal data compared to other techniques. In particular, it's shown that EPS can successfully identify model-dependent attacks and covert attacks that target control functions. Moreover, it's demonstrated that EPS can be used to detect previously seen attacks that weren't previously known. This work also identifies areas for improving EPS, including its application in model-agnostic scenarios and dealing with data loss, delays, and other practical problems that arise in real-world settings. Potential solutions for these issues are proposed, and further research is identified. This work is available at: https://github.com/afsharlab/eeps-surveillance. We address the challenge of identifying the intervention impact on a specific variable, Y, caused by a different variable, X, given that multiple interventions can occur with varying effects. To achieve this goal, we develop a framework for simultaneously testing multiple intervention questions while maintaining strict control over false discovery rate and accounting for data dependencies. To demonstrate our approach's effectiveness, we create a new class of graphical models, known as X-Y-Z models, to illustrate the complex interactions between variables, where X, Y, and Z are correlated with each other. We then conduct a comprehensive analysis of real-world experimental data from Amazon's Mechanical Turk to illustrate our approach's practical applications, particularly in extensive experiments. To this end, we investigate twenty different intervention questions to determine which shipping methods, including plain air and air with handling, significantly affect customer ratings on a particular product, given that ratings are influenced by various factors such as expected delivery time and order size. Utilizing our approach, we successfully control the false discovery rate and pinpoint the shipping methods that have a statistically significant impact on customer ratings, including the finding that slower shipping methods are preferred by customers even if they take longer to deliver. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to a broad range of intervention impact identification problems, particularly in fields where multiple interventions occur with varying effects and data is subject to dependencies and constraints. To facilitate replication of our results, we provide access to the raw data, a detailed description of our methods, and a series of computational experiments that validate our approach, including against a competing method that fails to control the false discovery rate and results in a false positive rate of 20%. Our findings highlight the importance of using our approach, which offers significant benefits over competing methods that fail to account for data dependencies and the critical role of false discovery rate control in intervention impact identification applications. Ultimately, our approach successfully identifies intervention impacts on highly dependent and constrained data while maintaining strict control over false discovery rate at or below any acceptable threshold. To further illustrate our approach's effectiveness, we conduct a series of computational experiments that demonstrate its statistical power and false discovery rate properties against a range of intervention impact identification problems with varying levels of data dependencies and constraints. Our approach is publicly available at https://github.com/crjones/fdr_influence. Our empirical results suggest that our approach is highly effective in identification intervention impacts while maintaining strict control over false discovery rate and is applicable to a range of statistical models including those with dependent and constrained data. To facilitate its use, we provide a public access to our approach at https://github

To accommodate large-scale cosmological data, I propose a modified model of dark energy with a density Ω_Λ of 0.72. I also suggest introducing a new parameter, n, to represent the rate of exponential expansion, set at 1 to align with observations of the Hubble constant. These adjustments contribute to the six-parameter Lambda-CDM model, which is supported by a fit to six independent observables: the deuterium pinching parameter, the acoustic scale, the temperature of the cosmic microwave background, the redshift of the cosmic microwave background, the brightness distance of type Ia supernovae, and the expansion rate of the cosmic microwave background. Additionally, I present a new inflationary scenario inspired by the Lambda-CDM model, with the potential to resolve discrepancies between local and cosmic measurements of the Hubble constant. Finally, I outline a possible connection between the inflationary scenario and the observed anisotropic expansion. Although the model does not resolve the discrepancy between local and cosmic Hubble constants, it is consistent with the cosmic microwave background data. In the context of the inflationary scenario, the discrepancy may be addressed at the semi-global scale, specifically between the Earth and the cosmic microwave background, rather than locally. This study presents methods for analyzing multidimensional non-stationary time series that contain rare, heavy-tailed disturbances. A linear time-trend framework is assumed, allowing for constant coefficients that may be adjusted periodically. A linear model with a mixed-norm (MN) approach is initially considered to analyze individual components, utilizing the mixed-norm norm to down-weight outliers. However, it's shown that this strategy can be less effective than other techniques in detecting structural changes. To address this limitation, a more versatile robust, heavy-tailed (RHT) estimation method is developed. The RHT approach yields more accurate results in various scenarios and is also capable of estimating the non-stationary components of the series. To achieve this, the RHT method differs from the MN by retaining (or setting) the norm components related to the time trend and lag variables, respectively. As a result, it's shown that RHT has superior performance in various scenarios and is also capable of estimating the non-stationary components of the series. To analyze the RHT estimator's accuracy, the study establishes asymptotic results for a broad class of multidimensional non-stationary time series. To put the RHT estimator to practical use, the study recommends a practical estimation strategy, known as the 'elimination and normalization strategy' (EAS), which is based on the average of RHT estimates derived from various 'normalizations' of the time series. A simulation study that mimics real-world data shows that RHT performs well in different scenarios. Furthermore, the study applies the RHT method to several financial time series. A practical implementation of the RHT method is also made available as an R package called 'InferRobTS'.

Neural radiance fields (NeRF) produce photo-realistic images by using volume rendering from pre-captured pixels. However, they require a dense set of images, often obtained through expensive time-of-flight cameras or extensive scanning, which can be difficult to access in certain situations. The alternative, deep learning-based methods that generate images from a single pixel, while efficient, fail to produce high-quality multi-scale images, resulting in low visual quality when used for tasks such as generating images of artwork or clothing that have been altered over time.

Our proposed model, the brightness field neural network, is a first attempt at developing a technique to store NeRF geometry and lighting information for dynamic objects. By introducing a brightness representation that is invariant to view and object rotation, and retaining the geometry information of individual frames, our system can generate high-quality images of objects that have been altered over time from a single pixel. When evaluated on a range of challenging out-of-distribution tasks, our system demonstrated superior performance to existing methods, and when used in a live setting to capture a couple's first kiss, our system produced results that were indistinguishable from real-life images. Our framework relies on partial video labels and image tags to identify key actions within videos and classify their associated context. However, existing image representations are inadequate for this task, and leveraging our knowledge of image labels in a meaningful way poses a significant problem. To address this issue, we propose IP-GCN, a graph convolutional network architecture that integrates partial video features with image labels, effectively capturing context information. By exploring the relationship between key action regions and image tags, IP-GCN bridges the gap between action detection and image recognition. Our framework consists of a multi-part design: (1) an attention-based graph convolution module to fuse key action spatial features with image semantic information, (2) an image tag graph built from human-annotated image categories to guide context capture, and (3) a localized activation graph based on key action regions to improve context information extraction from image tags. Evaluations on ActivityNetv1.0 and THUMOS-14 demonstrate that our context information extraction method outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches, with notable gains of +3.1% and +4.9% on ActivityNet and THUMOS-14, respectively. The SPH method has made significant advancements over recent years, addressing its core limitations one by one. Despite substantial progress, solving multi-phase fluid-structure interaction problems remains a multi-scale challenge for SPH researchers. Presently, there is a lack of a holistic, multi-scale SPH framework that can efficiently simulate a wide variety of physical models, encompassing thin elastic structures, incompressible fluids, compressible gases, and complex multi-phase flows. To bridge this gap, we developed a novel, multi-scale SPH framework capable of handling fluid-structure interactions across multiple physical models. This framework is particularly suitable for multi-phase flows, encompassing fluid-structure interactions, fluid-gas interactions, and gas-gas interactions. We compared our approach with existing methods using benchmark tests, such as the penetration test, buoyancy test, water incompressibility test, and a multi-phase flow test around an elastic cylinder. Furthermore, we demonstrated the practical application of our framework using a submarine example that involved multi-phase and fluid-structure interactions. This example showcased the ability of our framework to efficiently simulate complex multi-scale physical models with high accuracy. Results indicate that our framework achieves exceptional results, significantly outperforming existing methods in terms of accuracy at minimal computational cost. This framework offers a wide range of potential areas of improvement, making it an excellent starting point for further SPH advancements in the future. The presented framework, along with accompanying code and data, is available at https://github.com/MohammadMurtaza/Multi-scale-SPH. This resource serves as a valuable starting point and can be used to efficiently simulate various physical models with the suggested framework. Additional information can be found on the supplementary website at https://murtazaspl.github.io/Multi-scale-SPH. The SPH framework presented here has the potential to accelerate future SPH developments, promoting a domino effect of innovations and advancements in the SPH research community. Ultimately, this framework can efficiently simulate complex multi-scale physical models with high accuracy and minimal computational cost. A new approach called quantum assisted learning utilizes quantum computers to process machine learning data, which has recently shown improved performance in data analysis. The field of quantum assisted learning is rapidly evolving with emerging research and experiments. We conduct a comprehensive study on a quantum circuit learning framework, inspired by the original AAFF framework, utilizing 7-qubit superconducting processors. Our results compare the efficacy of single layer quantum neural networks in solving two classification tasks, which involve extracting patterns from random and highly disordered data. By leveraging quantum circuits that are either unmonitored or monitored, we evaluated the capacity of our qubit-based systems, specifically the role of coherence and with sampling rates. The findings indicate that despite shorter coherence times in hardware implementation, quantum assisted learning can achieve optimal results with minimal loss, which is resistant to degradation due to noise. The success of our study lays the groundwork for future research in advancing the applications of quantum computers in machine learning. This research presents an advanced technique for pitch augmentation called timbre-preserving pitch augmentation. Existing pitch augmentation methods can make speech more manageable for users with speech disorders, but they have been limited by a poor understanding of how pitch affects speech. To address this, a dataset of humans reading through a window of 1.5 seconds was used to train a neural model called FastPitch. This model was then modified using timbre-preserving pitch augmentation, which involves adjusting pitch while preserving the natural characteristics of the speaker's voice. The technique successfully improved the manageability of pitch in speech, according to user evaluations. Furthermore, a psychometric function was used to model how users with certain speech disorders respond to varying pitches. This function revealed a significant shift in the optimal pitch range for users with spasmodic speech disorder. Notably, the timbre-preserving pitch augmentation approach yielded more natural-sounding modifications when compared to a less sophisticated pitch augmentation method. While these modifications were well-received, users expressed a preference for unpitched speech over augmented pitch. Ultimately, the manageability of pitch in speech remains a complex issue, and a deeper understanding from speech-pathology experts is needed to develop highly effective pitch augmentation methods. Despite this, a well-developed research approach, incorporating both human-labeled datasets and psychometric function modeling, may lead to the creation of pitch augmentation methods that are tailored to the unique needs of individuals with specific speech disorders. The technique presented in this study has the potential to be a useful tool for creating personalized speech augmentation methods. The author notes that a major limitation of their approach is that it does not account for individual variations in pitch preferences. A potential solution to this issue is to train a neural model to predict the optimal pitch for a given individual, based on a large collection of user responses to varying pitches. This would enable the development of speech augmentation methods that are tailored to the unique preferences of each individual, rather than relying on a single-prediction model. The author's research has been applied to the creation of personalized speech augmentation methods, and a related study is currently in progress. The research has not been used to create a public dataset, as the author notes that the primary goal of their work is to develop an effective speech augmentation method, rather than contributing to the advancement of language models. However, a public dataset consisting of user responses to varying pitches could be used to train a neural model to predict the optimal pitch for a given text, and this could lead to the creation of a public dataset with actionable information. anchoring points without additional training. To assess our method's effectiveness,

Hopper achieves significant improvements in elevation estimation and adaptability
when compared to other models. To facilitate further research, we provide the
STC-Elevation dataset and Hopper's implementation for public use. Our work
contributes to the machine learning community in two key ways: first, we
identification of the value of multi-hop transformer models in spatiotemporal

issues. Our code is available at https://github.com/asharakeh/hopper. To access

Using robots for remote control via the internet, allowing users to control devices remotely, has become an area of interest. To gauge the quality of service provided by this technology, a new method of measuring user experience has been introduced. This research focuses on the service quality of remote control internet robots by defining a user experience metric and proposing an interactive approach to evaluate it. To this end, a large-scale experiment was conducted where 20 individuals remotely controlled a robot through a variable-quality internet connection while assessing their viewing experience. The results revealed how the control internet's quality impacted the users' perceptions and the role of the display in this perception, leading to a new quality of experience model. Based on this, a method to measure the quality of experience by simulating different network conditions in a laboratory setting was developed. The results demonstrated that this method effectively captures the influence of control internet quality on QoE and that the display plays a crucial role in this perception, while also showing that users can effectively assess qualitative service metrics without specialized training. The study's outcomes provide valuable insights for Service Providers to tailor their human-robot interactions to achieve the best possible quality of experience. Additionally, a publicly accessible simulation tool was created to enable researchers and Service Providers to assess and improve the quality of experience provided by remote control internet robots. The tool allows for simulations to be run with different network conditions and can be used to demonstrate how these conditions affect the quality of experience experienced by users. The study was published in a conference paper and presented at a workshop in 2021, while the underlying data was made available to the research community through a dataset published in 2022, which includes all experimentally determined QoE data, network characteristics, and simulation results. The study's findings were further showcased in a media publication that highlighted how the control internet's quality impacts the quality of experience and provided relevant examples, while the study's outcomes were also presented at multiple events including a workshop in 2021 and a conference in 2021, where the underlying concepts and ideas were discussed in depth. The study's outcomes were also awarded the Best Demo Paper Prize at a conference in 2021. We've developed a comprehensive model of The Mafia game, taking into account all its rules and player behaviors. In this model, a game lasts for a set number of days, each consisting of two phases. During the first phase, players can gather information about each other, align themselves with either the mafia or the civilians, and make a move. Mafias and the mayor can execute, while civilians can investigate or do nothing. Each day, one of two conditions is met - either a civilian is killed or a mafia member is killed. If the mafias' numbers haven't been diminished, they declare night. If the opposite is true, the day turns into night. Investigation results are made public, and players can use this information to align themselves with the opposing team. This model also considers the mafias' ability to lie when providing information. As a result, both teams try to eliminate the opposing team's members, while also attempting to maintain their own. Due to its complexity, this model is best analyzed using numerical simulations. Our study found that the likelihood of victory is influenced by both the game's duration and the number of mafias. Notably, this effect depends on whether the mafias are able to see the day or night. In the former case, an increase in mafias' numbers is associated with a decrease in the likelihood of victory for both teams. In the latter case, an increase in mafias' numbers is associated with a greater chance of victory for the mafias. Moreover, this model is resistant to simplification. For instance, it cannot be treated as a battle of two opposing forces. In fact, this model is characterized by an asymmetry of information, with the mafias possessing private information, while the civilians do not. In general, the likelihood of victory for the civilians is influenced by their ability to make the right choices at the right time, while the mafias' victory is contingent upon their ability to remain undetected. In the long run, the ratio of victories is approximately 50:50. On the other hand, an increase in the game's duration or the number of mafias results in a long-term victory ratio that deviates from 50:50. In the case of a long and short night, the ratio of victories is approximately 60:40 and 40:60, with the mafias being the victorious party. In the case of a medium-long night, the ratio of victories is approximately 55:45.

This study focuses on the simultaneous growth of two massive planets and its impact on their development and the surrounding protoplanetary disk. We utilized a detailed numerical model for a short period of 1 million years, starting when the planets form simultaneously from an equal division of disk mass at their respective radii. The results show a unique pattern of gas accumulation around the planets due to a spiral shock caused by orbital differences. The faster-orbiting planet accumulates gas, but the spiral shock eventually collapses due to a combination of factors including viscous dissipation, potential disk gaps, and interactions with smaller particles, leading to a transfer of gas to the slower-orbiting planet. However, the gas balance is consistently restored as the spiral shock re-forms. The model indicates that planet masses tend to converge over a period of 500-800 years. The research also demonstrates that the gas accumulation rate and final masses of the planets are influenced by factors such as the viscosity of the disk and the potential for formulating dust gaps in the presence of a high level of turbulence. The models predict that, under highly turbulent conditions, the final masses of the planets will be similar to those observed in the Solar System, approximately 10 Earth masses, while a relatively low level of turbulence may result in significantly more massive planets, potentially exceeding 100 Earth masses. Furthermore, the simulation reveals that the presence of massive planets and subsequent gas accumulation may cause the spiral arms to disappear and result in an inward migration of the planets and a corresponding increase in disk thickness due to the reduced viscous dissipation. The final mass configuration of the planets is found to be highly dependent on various factors, including the initial conditions of the disk and the complex interactions between the accretion process and the evolution of the disk. Consequently, a highly flexible and interactive model is required to accurately capture the competition for gas accumulation between planets and the co-evolution of the planets and the protoplanetary disk. The model suggests that a final mass of approximately 10 Earth masses may be a natural outcome for massive planets in disks with relatively low turbulence, while high levels of turbulence may result in significantly more massive or less massive planets beyond the critical threshold for massive accretion. The research implies a link between the final mass of the planets and their orbital configuration, suggesting that planets and the disks they form from may be subject to a competitive process where the configuration of the orbital paths may influence the final mass of the planets and the surrounding disks. In various scientific fields, identifying distinct clusters within mixed data remains a pressing issue. We present a novel fuzzy k-means approach to tackle this challenge, which adapts the entropy-based feature weighting from Huang et al.'s work to prioritize key dimensions for clustering. Unlike traditional methods, this algorithm can effectively handle high-dimensional information with an arbitrary number of features. We also introduce a compact representation of the data set as well as a performance evaluation criterion. Experimental results on artificially created data sets demonstrate the reliability and effectiveness of this algorithm. Moreover, its applications in gene expression data analysis and remote sensing imagery processing have been successfully implemented. Comparison studies with seven other algorithms highlight the reliability and competitiveness of this new method. [Published in: Knowledge-Based Systems, 2022]

The Mixture-of-Experts model has been a highly influential paradigm in probabilistic neural networks, yet its original variants were plagued by algorithmic difficulties that limited their practical use. In response, several dynamic programming algorithms have been proposed to circumvent these challenges, albeit at the expense of model simplifications or computational inefficiencies. In this work, we identify the specific issues that arose from MOE's local likelihood assumptions and derive a straightforward, two-stage solution to directly optimize the model parameters. This approach enables an exact, iterative fitting of even complex MoE models, including those with large numbers of experts, by directly tackling the inherent combinatorial complexity. Additionally, we address the local optimization problem with a global Konno-Takahashi algorithm, allowing for a comprehensive, non-local fit of MoE models. Our results demonstrate that these algorithms produce superior performance on a range of baseline tests, outperforming the state-of-the-art performance of Non-Local Mixture-of Experts in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. Moreover, the derived algorithms form the foundation for a series of novel, highly efficient MoE variants that surpass the state-of-the-art performance-accuracy trade-off. These variants, which include models with non-local data-driven expert boundaries, non-local gating networks, and hierarchical layers, are particularly well-suited to applications in non-local image denoising and deblurring. Overall, our approach enables a robust, efficient, and highly scalable solution to the MoE model that unlocks its full potential. This solution is particularly significant, given the numerous applications of MoE models that were previously simplified to circumvent computational issues. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexkamber/GloMoE. As a consequence of our work, we believe that this code will greatly contribute to the development of novel MoE-based methods and applications in the future. Furthermore, we anticipate a wide range of potential future applications, including the use of MoE models in generative neural networks, the development of unsupervised learning strategies, and the exploration of new MoE-based models that are informed by their non-local properties. These potential future contributions are highly promising and provide a theoretical foundation for their development. Finally, we believe that this work has significant implications for the use of MoE models in sparse modeling and related machine learning paradigms, given the local simplifications that were previously applied to circumvent computational issues. Our approach enables a robust, efficient, and highly scalable solution to the MoE model that unlocks its full potential in these areas

This study examines a broad class of games known as token-firing games, which encompass traditional reachability games as a specific case, using the framework of covering assignments and Jacobian matrices or, alternatively, covering assignments and intermediate structures called Prims varieties to gain insights. A substantial finding in this research is the identification of a distinct game category, which we term strongly reachable token-fairs, that can be characterized by a specific type of matrix rank condition in relation to a game's turn-based sequence. A key outcome of this characterization is a method for calculating a winning strategy for strongly reachable token-fairs using a well-defined set of tokens and a one-dimensional game structure, which can be achieved through a linear system of calculations related to a game's covering assignments and its prime structure. This strategic calculation method can be applied not only to strongly reachable token-fairs with one dimension but also to reachability games that are strongly reachable with any dimension. Moreover, a major outcome of this research is the establishment of a direct relationship between covering assignments and a game's prime structure, which enables the direct use of cover assignments to analyze prime structures, which has previously been a difficult task. A new approximation algorithm for token-firing games of cover assignment degree three is also presented and shown to have an exponential time complexity. This algorithm's performance is in contrast to the existing exponential lower bound of cover assignment degree two games, which is still the current best lower bound for this game category. Lastly, the study examines a multi-player version of token-firing games, which we term multi-player token-firing games, and a key finding in this area is the identification of a distinct multi-player game category, which is known as two-player reachable token-fairs, that can be characterized by a specific type of matrix rank condition in relation to a two-player game's turn-based sequence. By questioning long-held assumptions, we demonstrate that a widely accepted framework for assessing model transferability may be flawed and that current methods for measuring model robustness are inadequate. Through our analysis, we identify key limitations of the widely adopted Jacobian norm criterion for evaluating AT criterion for assessing model transferability. We show that this criterion is easily manipulable by data augmentation methods, which can result in misleading interpretations of a model's robustness. Furthermore, we find that JAC criterion is unable to account for the complex interactions between classes, which can limit its effectiveness in a multi-class classification setting. To address these shortcomings, we develop an alternative approach to assessing model transferability, utilizing the widely recognized entropy-based class activation map (CAM) to analyze how class interactions impact a model's decision-making processes. Through our examination, we uncover key insights that can inform the assessment and evaluation of deep neural network models. Our findings and code are publicly available at https://github.com/whwu1999/Rethinking-on-Transfer-Learning. Our findings indicate that density fluctuations can stimulate or hinder pebble dynamics, depending on the scale of the fluctuations. 

In the case of large-scale fluctuations, we observed a negative impact on pebble accretion, as high-density regions become isolated and pebbles are distributed more uniformly.

In the case of small-scale fluctuations, we observed a positive impact on pebble accretion, as dense regions serve as rapid conveyor belts for pebbles, facilitating gas giant planet formation.

The transfer of data from relational systems to RDF databases includes several key stages: first, data is stored in relational systems using concepts like tables and columns; next, RDF databases organize data as graphs with nodes and edges and specify data schema using shape expressions. Shape expressions define expected data patterns for RDF nodes, including properties and values. To facilitate data transfer from relational systems to RDF databases, several techniques such as SPARQL constructors and shape expression generators for RDF data transfer have been developed but often overlook key features like reference reuse and incomplete results. To address these limitations, two main issues with existing techniques need to be resolved: first, relational data patterns must be accurately assessed to ensure they align with shape expressions, considering factors like reference reuse; second, data transfer techniques must handle incomplete results without compromising data transfer. To overcome these challenges, this study introduces two essential tools: a language for describing relational data patterns that accounts for reference reuse and incomplete results, and a transfer algorithm that ensures these patterns align with target shape expressions. To validate this approach, this study performed comprehensive evaluations on diverse relational data patterns and shape expressions. Additionally, this study provides an implementation of the proposed technique and evaluates its performance compared to existing solutions. Experimental results demonstrate that, in general, the proposed method matches or surpasses existing best practices, but may fall short in complex cases with nested data. Notably, while other methods struggle with these patterns, they excel with simpler cases, resulting in comparable or better performance overall. Finally, the proposed technique is expected to serve as a foundation for future adaptations, such as developing refined transfer algorithms that can handle complex cases. As an open-source contribution, the authors implemented the proposed technique in DB2RDF, integrating it with existing data transfer methods like DB2RDF-Batch and SP2R. To facilitate future enhancements, the authors provide access to this source code along with shape expression generators through their online platform at db2rdf.org. Additionally, the authors organize and maintain the RDF data transfer community, including maintaining RDF data transfer best practices and related projects like RDF data transfer benchmarks and generators, and related codebases on GitHub. With this collective effort, the authors aim to support future advancements and integrate the proposed technique into widely-used tools like OpenRDF and SPARQL. As such, the authors welcome future adaptations and contributions from the community to expand upon this work and advance the state of the art in relational to RDF data transfer. Following standard community guidelines, the authors provide a comprehensive explanation of the proposed technique, along with detailed community involvement and contribution

In embedded real-time systems, the primary issue is minimizing the overhead of non-real-time applications while preserving real-time guarantees. Traditional virtualization solutions compromise either real-time performance or isolation. This research introduces a new hypervisor for embedded systems that takes advantage of the hardware virtualization assistance provided by the latest processors to address the limitations of previous approaches. A dual-bus mechanism is proposed to separate guest memory mappings from host memory mappings to ensure efficient resource sharing. To achieve this, the T-Visor hypervisor uses direct memory mapping and provides hardware support for interrupt handling, memory management, and I/O management, thereby allowing real-time performance and flexible resource allocation for non-real-time applications. A case study demonstrates that T-Visor outperforms existing solutions by providing superior real-time performance and better resource sharing for mixed importance embedded real-time systems. A prototype implementation is available to facilitate practical evaluations. A formal evaluation is presented to show that T-Visor's overhead is within the safe range for safety-critical systems. The evaluation is further validated through practical benchmarks, which show that T-Visor performs well in various scenarios, providing real-time performance and efficient resource allocation for non-real-time applications. Digital panoramic stitching is a common technique used in various applications, including virtual reality, navigation systems, and surveillance cameras. It is often employed by handheld or head-mounted devices that capture scenes from multiple viewpoints. Considering that users typically hold their devices with the camera facing downwards, given by the force of gravity, we propose a novel method that simplifies the stitching process by leveraging known 3D scene geometry and fundamental matrix constraints. This approach provides a reliable and efficient solution, even in scenarios where traditional methods rely on unreliable homography matches. Furthermore, we introduce a new performance metric that measures the panoramic sequence quality and evaluates the performance of various techniques in sequence initialization. Through both synthetic and real-world data analysis, we demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency on various datasets, including new panoramic sequences that are designed to push the limits of existing techniques. Additionally, we showcase the practical application of our approach in real-time surveillance scenarios, where it surpasses the current state-of-the-art by up to 2.5 seconds. Lastly, we showcase the practical application of our approach in a real-time camera setup with a 12 megapixel camera, capable of capturing around 20 frames per second. Overall, our approach provides a reliable, efficient, and practical solution to panoramic stitching that outperforms existing techniques.
