Research into designing resilient flight controllers using nonlinear models has grown in the last few years. For these controllers to be used in practical situations, they need to be able to withstand uncertainties in the model, including parameters that are hard to measure. This study focuses on developing a policy-based approach for designing resilient flight controllers that can adapt to uncertain parameters, including unobservable flight conditions. Nonlinear dynamic models with parametric uncertainty and model-mismatch errors have been used, incorporating Brownian motion and mass-spring dynamics for simulation purposes. A stochastic model-based method combining Monte Carlo simulation and model predictive control has been developed to generate controllers that can withstand parameter fluctuations. This method integrates real-time disturbance rejection and long-term policy optimization. Simulation results show that this method yields controllers with minimal oscillations and better robustness capabilities, including a 50% reduction in performance degradation under model mismatch compared to traditional methods. Additionally, the method allows for policy transfer, enabling a single controller to perform well in multiple scenarios with different parameter settings. This has the potential to reduce the time and cost associated with testing controllers in practical scenarios. Our method also surpasses existing approaches in this direction by providing a theoretical guarantee of optimality, including a 10% improvement in performance with no optimality guarantee observed in the model-free setting. This method has been tested using various flight scenarios with positive results, including scenarios where the flight model contains uncertainties in the wind and with simulated disturbances. Our study shows that policy-based approaches can be highly effective for designing resilient flight controllers, including a 50% improvement in performance with no tuning of the optimization solver. This has the potential to contribute to the development of more robust flight controllers in the future. meaning it's inherent and can't be overcome through spacetime's internal structure. 
In contrast, the negative curvature of negative mass spacetime is overcome 
when reached, while positive curvature is overcome before reaching the spacetime 
of a positive energy mass. The solitary nature of spacetime's curvature was 
first noted by Hawking and Ellis in their 1986 book, though it seems to have 
been largely overlooked in subsequent physics literature. This paper presents an 
initial examination of solitary spacetime curvature from a gravitational 
perspective, with a focus on its implications for energy and momentum 
interactions. The findings suggest that curvature is critical to the formation 
of gravitational force between energy entities. This discovery may lead to a 
reconsideration of energy and momentum interactions, with particular focus on 
the potential for unmanifest momentum. Manifest momentum requires a minimum 
curvature threshold, below which the momentum remains unmanifest. This 
threshold serves as a fundamental unit for measure, with potential to be 
further explored in future research. The article also delves into the 
interconnections between energy, momentum, and curvature, with suggestions 
that curvature is essential to the transfer of energy and momentum. As a 
result, the findings may contribute to a broader understanding of energy and 
momentum interactions. The present state of analysis indicates that while 
manifest momentum can exist without changes in energy, the momentum remains 
unmanifest without a change in curvature threshold. This relationship could be 
further dissected and analyzed in future research. The article also serves as 
a starting point for the exploration of fundamental gravity, energy, and momentum 
phenomena. The author aims to continue in this vein, with a broader vision of 
reexamining fundamental physics from a unique perspective in future work. The 
manifestation of unmanifest momentum may serve as a key test of this 
reexamination. The article can be accessed at arXiv:2111.16567. The associated

manifestation of unmanifest momentum, in particular, can be triggered by the 
change of curvature threshold as detailed on the website. The author can be

To achieve this, we have identified a universal formula for computing multipole expansions using the BMS algebra framework. We have shown that our general command principle includes all established soft formulas as special cases. We have used our method to derive new amplitudes and reviewed known ones, and we have demonstrated its applicability to a variety of processes including Higgs production and top decay. Furthermore, we have developed a novel formula for computing multipole expansions in annihilation processes. To validate our results, we have performed detailed analyses at the next-to-leading order and compared them to existing results in the literature. We have also identified opportunities for further research. Ultimately, we have demonstrated that our command principles provide a powerful tool for computing amplitudes and identifying universal contributions to observables. We have performed a thorough analysis of the subleading soft terms in QCD and identified universal and non-universal terms. We have shown that universal terms are determined by the BMS algebra, while non-universal terms depend on specific process details. Interestingly, our analysis reveals that some non-universal terms may potentially cancel out in observables. We have also derived a universal formula for calculating corrections to observables under variations of the radiation field. Continuous learning in real-world applications is inevitable, covering a wide range of scenarios, from image classification based on time-stamped data to tabular domains. Current research often assumes access to time-stampped data or groups data after training, but real-world problems often pose challenges such as shifting concepts or available training data being limited. To tackle these issues, there's a need for methods that don't make these assumptions and instead, consider the entire training process as a single continuous sequence. Such approaches, if they existed, would learn concepts in real-time without any interruptions, including during training and without any offline access to past data. To this end, we propose a novel online method that doesn't require data grouping or offline access, and is applicable to a wide range of image classification problems, including those with shifting concepts. By utilizing a neural buffer size of just 10,000 data points and having no memory for past steps, we were able to achieve state-of-the-art results, surpassing even offline methods that don't make any assumptions. Our results show that by integrating a novel clustering technique that adapts to the data in real-time, we are able to match the results of existing methods that group data before training. Human intestinal parasitic infections are a significant global health concern, and
categorizing intestinal worms from stool samples is the initial step in managing
these infections. This process can be challenging due to the similarity in features
of parasites and the variety of possible outcomes. To address this issue, a deep
learning approach using Stacked Autoencoders and Deep Belief Networks is presented
for classifying intestinal parasites. Features were extracted from digitized stool
sample images via Stacked Autoencoders, which were then used in Deep Belief Networks
for classification. This method achieved a success rate of 86% in a dataset of 698
images, comprising four parasite species. To facilitate widespread adoption in
resource-constrained settings, a simplified implementation of the model was also
developed and tested, demonstrating comparable performance to the original model. 
The source code for this project can be found on GitHub at 
https://github.com/arthai/Intestinal-Parasite-Classification-on-EBN-Net. This
research aims to increase awareness of intestinal parasitic infections and showcase
a practical solution for classifying intestinal parasites in resource-restricted
settings. This research was partly supported by the Brazilian Ministry of Science
and Technology's Young Scientist Program. Funding for digitization of parasite
images came from the FAPESP Digit project. All data for this research can be found
on https://github.com/arthai/Intestinal-Parasite-Classification-on-EBN-Net. This
research was supported by the Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São
Paulo, the Brazilian Ministry of Science and Technology's Young Scientist Program,
and the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development. The article

Producing temperature sky maps is an essential step for analyzing data from current and future experiments that observe the cosmic microwave background (CMB). Although several algorithms are available for this purpose, two main methods are widely used: mapmaking and forward modeling. The forward modeling approach, specifically maximum-likelihood estimation, is typically used to reconstruct temperature maps. The goal of this method is to achieve the highest probability of observing the CMB given the observed data. Post-processing techniques, like foreground subtraction and component separation, are used to recover the CMB. However, subtracting foregrounds can create an anisotropic "S-shaped" void around foreground sources on the map, which can affect the recovery of CMB parameters. This problem is particularly significant for projects like Simons Observatory, which must consider beam sizes carefully to avoid voids affecting CMB power spectrum reconstruction. We propose a novel approach, using a matched filter to enhance small-scale foreground estimation, which enables estimating foregrounds near powerful sources more accurately. The approach works by maximizing the likelihood of observing specific foreground patterns in data from individual sources. The method was tested using data from the BICEP/Keck collaboration and found to improve the estimation of foregrounds around bright sources. Furthermore, simulations showed that incorporating polarized foregrounds in this approach significantly improved the CMB power spectrum reconstruction compared to using two separate maps for temperature and polarization data. The method achieved better results than a common foreground subtraction algorithm, with a lower uncertainty in CMB $A_{\rm CC}$ of about 5%. The code used for these tests is part of the HEALPix Python package and can be used with future experiments to achieve more accurate CMB power spectrum reconstruction. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/healpix.sourceforge.net. This work was done as part of the Simons Observatory collaboration. The code used for foreground subtraction in this research had a bug that has now been corrected and submitted to the HEALPix Python maintenance team for consideration. The correction will ensure the code works correctly for subtracting foregrounds near sources, which may have had unintended consequences for experiments that use the code for data analysis. Specifically, previous versions of the code may have introduced systematic errors in CMB power spectrum reconstruction due to foreground subtraction artifacts. This theoretical framework has been further developed with a more comprehensive and fundamental approach. By applying the canonical transformation to four-dimensional space with a flat metric, a new constitutive relation has been derived for gravitational field propagation, displacing the Laplace equation and giving rise to an equation that is analogous to a wave equation in four-dimensional space. This constitutive relation has been experimentally confirmed and has a significant impact on cosmology, allowing space to be regarded as uniformly curved rather than flat, and suggesting a unifying approach to gravity rather than Newton's inverse square law. Moreover, this constitutive relation has a substantial application in resolving the twin paradox in special theory of relativity. In addition, several novel consequences have been proposed, including the detection of gravitational waves, the occurrence of gravitational redshift, and the association of gravitational intensity with energy flux. All of these proposed consequences have been experimentally confirmed, and it appears that the on-shell condition of this constitutive relation confers energy on the gravitational field, which has a mass proportional to energy flux. This constitutive relation has a significant impact on understanding black holes, which are not supernatural objects but rather a consequence of uniformly curved space that is beyond the event horizon of a star that has exhausted its energy, and the universe is not expanding because of translation motion that is consistent with Hubble's findings. Finally, several novel and profound implications have been proposed for constitutive relation physics in cosmology. In recent years, transformers have surpassed traditional recurrent models as the preferred architecture for sequence tasks. Despite transformers's inherent superiority in representation capabilities, they are outperformed by models incorporating separate generative networks in tasks such as density estimation and sampling. We address this disparity by proposing a hybrid architecture, where a transformer-based generative network is used in conjunction with a separate discriminator to determine the representation of a conditional input. Our method, which employs a mode-covering approximation of the generative network's output mode mixture distribution to facilitate representation learning, leverages a modified forward process to produce a consistent ordering of inputs, thereby simplifying the amortization of latent variables. Our experimental findings indicate that this architecture yields state-of-the-art results on the Meta World benchmark and demonstrates comparable performance to VQ-VAEs on the CIFAR10 dataset. Moreover, we observe that the representations learned by our model from synthetic data can effectively be utilized for downstream tasks without requiring retraining. Our research reveals that a standard transformer-based generative network is capable of generating effective representations, thus validating and clarifying the assumptions underlying the vanilla transformer architecture. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/j-terrell/the-profound-generative-decoder.

The task of predicting the intensity of specific emotions expressed in written text is a difficult case of aspect-based sentiment analysis.  This particular application has several unique demands, including the fact that certain emotions are rarely found in the dataset, and the associated words can be confusing - for instance, "love" can mean either a romantic feeling or a general affection.  Furthermore, since we're asked to determine the degree of a particular emotion related to a given aspect - for example, "how happy is the chef?" - we need to be able to distinguish between emotions even when they're expressed in very different ways.  To address this challenge, a new approach called LSHED is being proposed which stands for Learning Hidden Sentiment with Distinction Enhancement.  This approach involves a two-part training process.  Firstly, it trains a large language model with "soft" guidance to focus on the emotional content by asking it to distinguish between different emotions it's been labeled as expressing during the data pre-processing stage.  Secondly, it trains another model on top of this foundation with "hard" guidance to refine its ability to identify the degree of specific emotions in given contexts by only allowing it to make predictions that match the emotions it's been previously "marked" as expressing during the actual data training stage.  To enhance the model's ability to recognize emotions that are rarely found in the dataset, a part of the model is being refined with a special "negative sampling" technique.  To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, several experiments have been conducted which demonstrate that LSHED outperforms the existing state-of-the-art models by a significant margin on several popular datasets.  To further investigate the potential of the proposed approach, several experiments have been conducted which help to understand the impact of the "guided" training process on the model's performance - for instance, the results show that the proposed approach is highly sensitive to the "hard" guidance and needs to be refined with several iterations of model refinement.  To address this challenge, a part of the model is being refined with a special model tuning process.  To further understand the potential of the proposed approach, several experiments have been conducted which demonstrate that the proposed approach can be extended to handle more complex challenges such as identifying the degree of specific emotions in given contexts with additional noise and the presence of misleading words and characters.  To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, several experiments have been conducted which demonstrate that the proposed approach performs consistently better than the existing state-of-theart models on several metrics including F1-score

Recent research demonstrates that large language models have the ability to process images and use this information to generate text based on vision-guided prompts. However, current methods are unable to include complex text within the image, often resulting in poor performance on tasks such as vision-guided title creation. To address this limitation, we developed an approach that allows models to directly access and utilize text within image files by treating them as sequential byte streams. This involves encoding the text through tokenization and embedding it in token form, enabling models to integrate visual and linguistic information and create more accurate titles based on vision-based prompts. Experimental findings indicate that our method leads to significant improvements in title creation, producing titles that are 9.8% closer to the reference titles on COCO, 7.9% closer on Flickr8K, and 9.6% closer on Flickr102K. Notably, our method demonstrates generalizability across multiple language models with varying levels of performance. challenging. To aid in this process, a technique called brightness measurement is 
developed for evaluating light beams. This process involves precise measurement 
of two key light properties: its radiation spectrum and the distribution of photons 
within it. A software, known as Brightness Scans, was created to facilitate this 
evaluation. This tool was used to generate simulated light beams with predefined 
characteristics and calculate their brightness for reference. To validate the 
tool's effectiveness, it was applied to real-world light beams, including a specific 
test involving a UV-X undulator at the Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin. By comparing 
measured and calculated light characteristics, it was found that the tool accurately 
reproduced the measured data. This validation confirms the tool's effectiveness 
and its potential to support the analysis of light beams in applications and

Recent research on $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ decays, where $n=1,2,3$, has been performed to understand the decay properties of the recently discovered $\Upsilon(10753)$. These decays are unique because they don't involve any direct $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ transitions detected so far, and are instead driven by a hadronic loop process involving $M(10860)$. Our analysis reveals that $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(2S)\pi^+\pi^-,\Upsilon(3S)\pi^+\pi^-$ decays are dominated by two-loop processes involving $M(10860)$, while $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^-$ is primarily a three-loop process involving $M(10860)$. These results are further substantiated by predicted branching ratios, which suggest that $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(2S)\pi^+\pi^-,\Upsilon(3S)\pi^+\pi^-$ decays should be observable at Belle II and Belle II experiments, and that $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^-$ decays should be detectable at Belle II experiments. Ultimately, these findings highlight the significance of hadronic loop processes in understanding the properties of recently discovered heavy-quark bound states like $\Upsilon(10753)$. The study also underscores the value of $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(2S)\pi^+\pi^-,\Upsilon(3S)\pi^+\pi^-$ decays as crucial indicators of hadronic loop processes. Moreover, it indicates that $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^-$ decays could serve as a vital sign of complex loop processes. The study is further expected to inspire further research into the characteristics of $\Upsilon(10753)$ in experiments such as Belle II and LHCb, and to shed light on the importance of hadronic loop processes in understanding certain properties of $\Upsilon(10753)$. In graph computing, distance tagging is a widely used technique that assigns each vertex a brief description indicating its distance to closest neighbors. This process is highly versatile and applies to online Combinatorial Stream Pattern Matching (CSPM), where it enables real-time detection of periodic patterns or anomalies. To improve online CSPM, we propose a new method based on fault-tolerant distance tagging in graphs. This innovative approach reduces memory usage and operating costs in graph databases by leveraging a sparse set of tags. Planar graphs, with their neat layout and constraints, are our focus for this algorithm. By identifying key vertices and employing a sparse set of tags, we can ensure that the algorithm works even with faulty information. This approach is highly efficient, requiring only O(log n) memory and a constant number of operations, independent of the graph size. Experimental results show our algorithm can handle faults without increasing the operation count. Furthermore, the algorithm can detect all nearest neighbor vertices to any given vertex in O(log n) time. This breakthrough allows for the creation of a fault-resilient CSPM solver with low storage and processing costs. Our method can detect periodic patterns in a fraction of time and with a fraction of storage of standard algorithms. This technique is highly adaptable and can be applied to a variety of graph-based tasks. [Our Code is on Github] https://github.com/krivitski/apsp_dist_tagging/tree/fault_tolerant_dist_tagging. We analyze a class of second-order elliptic equations in divergence form, with high-measure currents as coefficients. These currents are represented as $W_{i,j}$ in $L^2(\Omega)$, along with boundary conditions on $\partial\Omega$. Our study focuses on two key outcomes: Firstly, it is demonstrated that the Dirichlet problem, with its prescribed boundary conditions and source term $f$, yields a weak solution for nearly all boundary conditions, except possibly on a set of measure zero. Secondly, for study of the oblique boundary problem, it is shown that weak $W^{1,p}$-solutions exist for almost all boundary conditions, except on a set of measure zero. These findings are achieved through the application of techniques for representing currents as $L^2$ functions and exploiting "smallness" conditions to determine density results for operators with singular coefficients. These results are also generalized for nonlinear elliptic equations. Our work is motivated by recent research findings in references \cite{CR14,CR18}. Furthermore, related results and an extension to the weak $W^{1,p}$-solvability of the oblique boundary problem for measure-valued boundary operators have been generalised in the author's PhD thesis \cite{K20}. Recent work has extended this framework to cover a broader range of statistical models, including distributional Gaussian process models. However, the existing notion of out-of-sample data in these models is unclear and lacks a coherent definition. To address this gap, a new learning theory is developed for machine learning to define out-of-sample data in a diverse set of Gaussian process models. A consistent definition is derived for these models, and it is applied to Gaussian processes, their extensions, and other related models. A data-driven criterion is also proposed to evaluate the goodness-of-fit of these models to data. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the out-of-sample detection problem can be framed as a minimax optimization task, and it is applied to a variety of distributional Gaussian process models. To facilitate practical implementation, two data-driven algorithms are proposed for this task, and they are tested in simulated case studies and real-world applications. We show that these algorithms can successfully identify out-of-sample data in a variety of contexts, and it is also demonstrated that the recently proposed machine learning approach can be used to derive novel results for classical Gaussian processes. To further validate the performance of these algorithms, a real-world application is conducted in the field of healthcare. We apply the out-of-sample detection task to COVID-19 data from several European countries, and it is also demonstrated that the derived models can be used to predict and understand out-of-sample data. Recent advancements in $O(a)$ improved lattice QCD calculations are reviewed, 
particularly those using Wilson fermions and domain wall fermions. While 
focus is on the low interaction strength regime, key findings such as those 
in chiral limit and at moderate interaction strengths are also discussed. The 
reviews cover updates in 2013, 2014 conferences held in Boston and Newark. 

The chiral limit results for Wilson fermions, including pion mass and decay 
constant, and quark mass and axial nucleon matrix element are presented. The 
calculations are performed using multiple variants of $O(a)$ improvement, 
including one-loop coefficients for Wilson action. The outcomes are compared 
to the situation where the lattice spacing is completely removed. The 
reliability of these results is examined through consistency checks on the 
temperatures and pressures calculated on ensembles with varying discretization 
effects. 

In addition to these results, an approach to perform calculations on fine 
lattices with physical quark masses, and hence without quark mass regularization 
on the lattice, is described for both Wilson and domain wall fermions. The 
approach is discussed for both SU($N_c$) gauge field ensembles with $N_c = 3$ 
and $N_c = 2$, including results for $N_c = 2$ obtained with four heavy quarks 
treated as valence quarks. 

Finally, some ongoing work is mentioned including further improvements to 
$O(a)$ improved lattice QCD calculations and investigations beyond the chiral 
limit. These investigations are based on Wilson fermions under specific conditions 
and the QCD action with non-zero $\kappa_{\rm Maj}$. Further details are also 
given on the publication list and collaboration members. 

The reviews cover updates in 2015 and 2016 conferences held in Newark and Boston.

in fast automatic differentiation and optimization procedures. Standard computations 
often involve complex algebraic manipulations with large matrix storage needs,

vertex-based approach for computing the curvature without the need for memory-intensive 
matrix storage. ViViT's effectiveness in MinimaMax and PyTorch shows significant 
cost reductions in training time for deep learning models, with particular advantages 
in memory-constrained environments. ViT's scalability and performance benefits have 
been demonstrated in context-free sequence modeling, graph auto-regressive models, 
graph information-networks, graph transformers, neural PDEs, geometry-based 
modeling, implicit modeling, low-shot learning, implicit embedding, few-shot 
learning and few-shot meta-learning. The code and findings are available on GitHub.

Estimating the precise 3D position of every class within an image is a critical
component of numerous applications in computer vision, notably autonomous driving
and robotics. Unlike previous approaches, we don't require prelabeled data or
manual adjustments, making our process highly scalable and efficient. Despite
absent feedback mechanisms, we've developed a technique that outperforms existing
similar methods and provides accurate positions for objects in an image. Our
technique relies on a direct estimation approach using a simple convolutional
model and relies solely on the output of a mask completion model to determine
position accuracy. Through comprehensive testing on the YOLO Baidu challenge
dataset and the KITTI dataset, we've shown that our model can achieve high
accuracy, with positions that are on average no more than 1.5 pixels off for some
object categories in the YOLO Baidu dataset. Moreover, we've extended this model to
estimate 3D positions in the KITTI dataset with results that show a mean distance
of less than 1m for some object categories. Current methods have significant
shortcomings, particularly with larger object categories in the KITTI dataset
where the estimated mean distance to ground truth is a least 0.8m. Interestingly,
our model's performance on the YOLO Baidu dataset's top 10 most frequent class
types shows that it significantly outperforms previous methods by an average of at
least 0.3m when estimating object categories in the KITTI dataset. Our code and
model are publicly available at https://github.com/andrearm/zero-shot-pose-est. This discrepancy can be attributed to the flow's rotational characteristics, specifically its prolateness and meridional shift, which significantly impact the rotation period at high latitudes and low depths. Light field technology captures the full pattern of light in a scene from a specific viewpoint, but its high dimensional data makes it computationally expensive to record and store. To overcome this challenge, researchers focus on practical light field image compression. While current advanced models offer improved quality, they fall short in real-world application due to their reliance on extensive training data and high compression ratios. In response, a new approach is proposed, incorporating a unique disparity-aware model that enables it to compress images on its own without needing vast training data. This model, paired with a novel practical compression framework, allows for efficient compression of any view. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, and it outperforms existing standard techniques in terms of view compression rate. When paired with a state-of-the-art model, the results show significant improvement in terms of PSNR and SSIM scores across all views. Moreover, the approach is shown to be effective in various practical light field capture scenarios, including light field microscopes and 3D scenes with significant depth. The corresponding code is available on GitHub at the specified repository address. This method offers a range of benefits, including improved view quality, increased number of views with the same compression ratio, and higher compression ratios for the same view quality compared to baseline methods. In terms of limitations, the approach performs optimally with a limited number of models trained on distinct datasets, and it tends to struggle with large depth disparities. To mitigate these issues, future research could focus on developing a single model capable of handling scenes with significant depth disparities, and it may also explore the use of model-agnostic techniques that don't require training on specific tasks. Ultimately, the proposed approach has the potential to significantly advance the state-of-the-art in practical light field image compression. This method is compatible with a range of platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS, and it utilizes a range of libraries including PyTorch, numpy, and torchvision. To demonstrate its practicality, the approach has been successfully applied to a micro-spectroscopy light field capture paradigm. Notably, the corresponding light field capture technology is currently being used in a state-of-the-art light field microscope at Stanford University. To visualize the effectiveness of the proposed method, the results can be viewed as a video or by using a VR headset. In the second part of our study on atmospheric scattering, we conducted a thorough examination of previously developed atmospheric models for use in the K-band. These models were created after analyzing off-axis observations of a reference bright source, for example the Moon, from two telescopes located in Paranal (17.42° S, 69.90° W) and San Pedro de Atacama (23.05° S, 66.16° W). We evaluated and compared the structure of the atmospheric models across different observatories, highlighting the models' discrepancies and suggesting ways to improve them. Additionally, we present a novel approach to characterize atmospheric models using differential observations, in which we compare the effects of atmospheric scattering on a reference source observed off-axis from two telescopes. This method yields a range of observables, including the apparent shift of the source, magnification, rotation angle, and ellipticity. It also enables the calculation of a scalar invariant related to the atmospheric scattering angle, offering a more complete characterization of atmospheric models. The method was successfully applied to observations of the Moon, a Galactic nucleus reference source, and the quasar 3C 273, and its results were used to determine the atmospheric scattering angle in the K-band for the ALMA telescope. The obtained information can be utilized to refine the positioning accuracy of telescopes, which is particularly essential for interferometric systems, and also provides essential data for wavefront correction via adaptive optics and helps to assess the performance of imaging and spectroscopic experiments in the K-band. The findings and methodologies presented in this work will be instrumental in preparing upcoming large-scale ground-based observatories for atmospheric conditions in the K-band. Federated learning allows multiple parties to collaborate on training models by sharing model updates, not raw data, which enables the creation of sophisticated machine learning models for applications such as mobile apps without compromising users' privacy. This paper delves into the challenges of achieving fairness and maintaining data confidentiality in federated learning. We propose a framework for ensuring that aggregated data from parties in federated learning meets a certain level of differential confidentiality. This requires each party to adhere to a principle of quantitative justice, where parties with different data volumes contribute updates proportionate to their inventory. We also introduce two concepts of differential confidentiality, known as $\epsilon$-confidentiality and $\text{cDPI}$-confidentiality, which can be seen as specific instances of a broader, more flexible measure of confidentiality. Based on these principles, we develop two methods for enhancing data confidentiality in federated learning. The first method involves selecting parties for training in each iteration to minimize information about individual parties, while the first method is combined with a technique of distributing training tasks among parties to optimize model accuracy in the face of uneven data distributions across parties. Our approach builds on existing fairness and confidentiality mechanisms in federated learning, which often assume that parties have balanced data sets but do not address the case where this is not so. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method using both artificial data and real-world examples from the dataset, which shows that it leads to substantial improvements in data confidentiality and accuracy in federated learning applications. The method is designed to be adaptable to a variety of scenarios and can be applied to a range of training algorithms, which expands the possibilities for collaborative machine learning across parties with unequal data distributions without compromising users' privacy. A graph invariant is considered substantial if the series of its associated polynomials exhibits stability under small perturbations. This concept is modelled after Tamarkin's concept of stability for families of linear maps. Key graph invariants providing examples of stable and unstable polynomials include the chromatic polynomial, the Jones polynomial, the Tutte polynomial, the Tutte-Grothendieck polynomial and the Bollob's ri-polynomial. Interestingly, the Tutte-Grothendieck polynomial lies on the boundary of this classification. Additionally, the properties of stable graph invariants can be used to derive a hierarchical relationship among these invariants, revealing that the Tutte-Grothendieck polynomial depends on the previously stable invariants, $\zeta$, and a new, stable invariant $\tau$. This relationship serves as the foundation for studying $\tau$ and exploring its applications in combinatorics and formal noncommutative algebra, as well as potentially leading to a new graph classification invariant with desirable properties. This research contributes to understanding the properties of unstable graph invariants and the interplay between stability, algebra and combinatorics. Furthermore, the paper investigates properties of $\zeta$ and $\tau$ in noncommutative algebra and demonstrates new relationships among graph invariants. It also derives formulas for $\zeta$ and $\tau$ in terms of $\mu$-invariants and identifies instances where $\tau$ reduces to known stable invariants. Ultimately, the paper proposes that the Tutte-Grothendieck polynomial could be the last invariant to become stable, paving the way for the construction of a new graph classification invariant with desirable properties. This work is an expansion on prior research, including a 2017 report and a 2020 preprint, which addressed similar concepts. Both documents can be accessed at the authors' websites.

Several models have been introduced to forecast long-term energy system development. Despite their popularity, there is a lack of research on model evaluation methods. This paper proposes a framework for examining the impact of various assumptions in models that analyze long-term energy systems. By applying this framework to PATH and TIMES models, which utilize linear programming, we identified key variables that can be modified to assess system development under different scenarios. These variables include technology improvement rates, energy resource prices, social costs of carbon, and regulatory policies. When we deviated from predefined assumptions in these models, we found significant changes in energy system design. This included shifts away from energy sources such as natural gas and towards hydrogen, changes in electricity generation, and varying levels of renewable energy. Furthermore, the study revealed that the spatial distribution of energy resources within models like SUPERTARGET significantly affects system design in multiple regions. These results underscore the need for comprehensive model evaluation approaches that consider various assumptions. By adopting such an approach, we can identify critical variables that can be modified to assess system development under different scenarios. This is particularly essential for decision-makers, researchers, and modelers working with static models of long-term energy systems. 

The method presented in this paper can be applied to models with linear characteristics, and we hope its extension to non-linear models will be achieved in future studies. Moreover, the study highlights the value of combining growth models with real options analysis to examine technology adoption risks and uncertainties. This, in turn, can inform the development of targeted policies and research agendas that take into account the assumptions underlying energy system forecasts. 

The final section of the paper discusses potential future avenues for model evaluation and feedback loops that can facilitate two-way communication between growth models and actual trends in energy systems. This is an area that requires further exploration to refine the accuracy and reliability of long-term energy system forecasts. 

In terms of model development, the study emphasizes the need for approaches that simulate a wide range of possible energy system trajectories to better capture the uncertainties and risks associated with these models. This is an essential consideration for decision-makers, as models that fail to account for uncertainty may recommend high-stakes investments with low likelihood of success. 

Lastly, the study highlights the importance of differentiated actor models that can motivate and influence other actors to adopt or refrain from certain energy technologies. This is an area that requires further exploration to better understand the role of individual and collective agency in shaping energy system design.

This method leverages pre-trained, cross-attention enhanced language models to compute summary quality based on explicit document-summary and query-document comparisons. Moreover, CrossSUMM outperforms existing metrics in a range of evaluations, including better correlation with human judgments on MS MARCO, Devenek and NewsSum, and superior performance in key retrieval and abstractive summarization tasks. To facilitate adoption, the code and pre-trained models for CrossSUMM are made publicly available. Finally, it is found that human editors' corrections can effectively guide the distillation of pre-trained language models, resulting in improved performance of TokenFID. The problem of applying a quadratic transformation to a complex multivariate signal and demodulating it at a known frequency is core to numerous signal processing techniques. This is an underdetermined problem, but it's often tackled by imposing sparsity on the signal phase, yielding the sixteenth power condition to guarantee unique solution restoration. Notably, research has shown that in the case of a simple sinusoid, a much weaker condition can guarantee N-dimensional signal phase restoration. This study aims to generalize the sinusoidal case to a quadratic transformation and a sinusoid surrogate, while imposing sparsity on the signal phase. By doing so, it achieves the phase locking property and restores the signal phase under a condition that is two times tighter than the sixteenth power condition. This breakthrough allows for the recovery of the signal phase in as few as N log(N) measurements over a finite period. Furthermore, it presents a method for obtaining the signal phase from a small number of measurements obtained over a short period by sampling a signal that undergoes a quadratic transformation at or above the signal sampling rate. This method does so with essentially the same number of measurements as sampling the signal itself and achieves a nearly optimal condition that is only a factor of two away from optimal. By employing sparsity, it obtains the signal phase with minimal bias. The findings were validated through experiments involving synthetic and real-world data, and comparisons with existing techniques showed that it outperformed them. This study provides the first proof that from as few as N log(N) measurements obtained over a short period, it is possible to restore the signal phase that undergoes a quadratic transformation. Recent advancements in Zero-shot Natural Language Inference (Zero-shot NLI) frameworks have demonstrated that language models can perform various natural language understanding tasks without using explicit training data, provided that the required dataset and prompt combinations are available. However, to improve model performance in Zero-shot NLI, we need to select an optimal dataset and prompt ensemble. To address this, the model parameters need to be adjusted based on performance metrics. However, since direct tuning is not feasible, infeasible tuning space, or model pre-training is not possible, we need to fine-tune the language model on the selected dataset and prompt ensemble. To solve this, we introduced Meta-tuning, a fast and efficient fine-tuning process that assembles an optimal dataset and prompt combination, and then fine-tunes the language model on it. We conducted two sets of meta-tuning experiments. The first experiment was based on model selection and involved meta-tuning the model on different dataset and prompt combinations to improve its performance on various benchmarks. The second experiment was based on cross-model adaptation and involved transferring the model's knowledge from a source dataset to a target dataset using meta-tuning. The results showed that meta-tuning was able to improve model performance by 4-15 points on various benchmarks, while requiring only a linear number of steps and linear number of parameters adjusted. In this study, we engage in a comprehensive analysis of the fundamental principles governing Kerr-lens mode-locking, with a focus on the role of Kerr-lens resonators in seed pulse formation. Through an in-depth investigation, we evaluate the relative merits of ring and linear resonators in conjunction with the σ-scan technique and assess their suitability for achieving high-energy pulse amplification. Ultimately, we provide practical guidelines for achieving ultrafast lasers that can generate exceptionally short pulses with high energy levels. Additionally, we present an innovative method for examining pulse formation within Kerr-lens mode-locked amplifiers, which does not rely on numerical simulations but rather geometrically models the pulse generation process within the σ-scan method. This approach provides a clear, easy-to-interpret pulse breakup regime that can be easily quantified. Furthermore, we present numerical results demonstrating the pulse energy capabilities of a high-peak-power Kerr-lens mode-locked amplifier, with the ability to achieve nearly 100 W of pulse energy at 30 fs, resulting in an impressive time-integrated energy density of 3.3 μJ. These findings are expected to significantly contribute to the development of high-energy ultrafast laser systems. Lastly, we outline the vast applications of high-energy, ultrafast lasers across diverse fields such as nonlinear spectroscopy, microscopy, imaging, nonlinear photonics, medical applications, surface processing, atomic physics, particle acceleration, and nonlinear optics. We investigate the statistical properties of a cover-based technique for option pricing developed by Bouchaud and Ghysel. This approach entails using a finite mixture of local risk-neutral density distributions to model the log-price of a financial asset. Specifically, we consider a situation where the components of this mixture are uniformly distributed around the current price, and we derive precise high-dimensional expansions for key option valuation parameters such as the call price and its Greeks. Our analysis reveals that the expansions rely on two main terms - the local asymptotic alpha Volterra expansion and a Black-Scholes expansion - and it enables the omission of lower-order terms. Furthermore, we apply the cover-based model to study the asymptotic behavior of the Greeks and to assess its numerical performance compared to the local expansions. Our results show that the cover-based model yields nearly the same precision as the local expansions in high-dimensional settings. This approach can also be extended to multivariate options and entails a comparable computational efficiency as the local expansions. Additionally, we observe that the cover-based model is versatile and can be used to model a wide range of financial quantities beyond option prices, such as quantities related to dividends and transaction costs. This model can potentially be applied to data analysis as well as provide valuable insights into the asymptotic behavior of financial quantities. Our method allows the cover-based model to pass statistical tests for goodness-of-fit, and it remains unaffected by the stochastic alpha model's shortcomings, which have been documented in the literature. Our research also reveals that the cover-based model's performance improves when incorporating a non-linear boundary, which is in contrast to the linear boundary used in the original cover-based model. We applied the cover-based model to a European put option and observed that its loss of accuracy compared to the local expansions increases by about 10% as the strike distance from the at-the-money zone grows. This increase in error is largely attributed to the omission of the second-order term in the local expansions. We applied the cover-based model to a diverse set of 16 distinct European options and observed that its numerical performance exhibits a consistent trend. We believe that the cover-based model's high accuracy and statistical robustness make it a strong candidate for real-time option pricing. Standard methods are ill-equipped to handle these scenarios due to their data-hungry approach. However, it's now clear that such networks are valuable and worth studying in their own right. Our research focuses on developing a new framework, called SSNE, designed specifically for sparse networks. Initially, we adapt a stochastic gradient descent approach to significantly reduce the number of data points required per node, making it more suitable for sparse networks. Our SSNE framework utilizes these minimized data points to train node embeddings, differentiating itself from prior methods by only employing local neighborhood data and introducing a new constraint to enhance training stability. To further enhance performance, we integrate a novel structural predictor based on node embeddings. Our empirical results demonstrate that SSNE outperforms existing node embedding methods and competing link prediction baselines on a range of sparse network types, including molecular graphs, web graphs, and social networks. Moreover, we find that SSNE node embeddings are universally applicable and align with prior findings on the degree-based prioritization of link prediction. Interestingly, we observe that SSNE achieves better performance compared to a prior method that relies on global degree pre-ranking. Additionally, we demonstrate that SSNE is capable of adapting to various network types and even performs better on synthetic networks with corrupted structural information. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/kuilu/SSNE. While SSNE excels in link prediction, it does so by leveraging node embedding techniques that may be broadly applicable to other node classification and graph mining tasks. Our findings provide insights on the stability and various advantages of node embedding training methods. Ultimately, SSNE's success on sparse networks has significant implications for various graph-related applications, and our code on GitHub could prove useful for mining such networks. It's worth noting that while SSNE performs well on synthetic networks with noise, it does not excel in predicting edges on test sets derived solely from noise, indicating that it still relies on structural patterns present in the training data. Our SSNE approach contributes to the development of efficient node embedding techniques that prioritize structural information while minimizing the need for data, differentiating itself from prior methods that often prioritize node attributes. Traditionally, nonlinear distortion in systems employing the Q-amplitude, Q-phase, and combined polarization modes (QP) format have been modeled using the PM-PM and PM-PDP models, where the former considers linear polarization mode coupling and the latter considers both linear and differential nonlinearity. This approach enables robust intent detection and representation learning, demonstrating better performance on real-world datasets. The antagonistic effect of self-supervised learning originates from the contrast between self-supervised and supervised learning susceptibilities. While self-supervised models are highly sensitive to data variations, supervised models struggle with subtle changes in data distribution. We investigate this phenomenon within the context of automatic speech recognition and suggest a new metric, called antagonistic susceptibility, to measure the antagonistic effect. Through semi-supervised settings for self-supervised learning, we demonstrate the antagonistic effect through experiments and provide insights into the optimal balance between self-supervised and supervised data for training models with improved generalization. We also address potential generalization issues by identifying the ideal point of balance and provide a new interpretation of the effect through the comparison of gradient norms. Our method enhances the understanding of self-supervised learning outcomes and provides a data-efficient training strategy for speech recognition systems. We also release our code on GitHub to facilitate replication. We also compare the effect of different pre-training objectives and find that the antagonistic effect is similar for different objectives but may vary based on the comparison method in the future. We address the challenge of deconvolving sparse signals buried in noise through inverse problems like seismic reflection inversion. To enhance sparsity, we introduce the non-uniform sparse model (NUM) and its log-likelihood. However, computing the optimal M-estimator is infeasible due to its non-differentiable and non-smooth nature. To approximate this in a differentiable and sparse-based framework, we propose the nuSPAN model, which adds Gaussian noise to NUM's log-likelihood. This allows us to train a proximal neural network by minimizing the total nuSPAN cost. By leveraging this network, we can derive an approximate M-estimator in a forward and efficient manner. Through numerical simulations on synthetic data, we demonstrate the effectiveness of nuSPAN in deconvolving Seismic traces and outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we showcase its ability to handle varying trigger rates in real-world data. Furthermore, we find that nuSPAN generalizes well to Seismic reflection inversion. To that end, we propose a novel extension of nuSPAN to two-dimensional Seismic data. This method can also be applied to other inverse problems involving non-uniform sparse signals. With the rise of deep learning in Seismic applications, nuSPAN offers a novel solution to tackle numerical challenges in this field. It can be used as a stand-alone method or in conjunction with existing sparse-based algorithms to speed up convergence. Moreover, we provide a mathematical proof that nuSPAN converges to a stationary point of the target optimization problem. This is a significant contribution as it bridges the gap between the NUM log-likelihood and a differentiable, sparse-based loss function. Many cities' residents anticipate high-quality public services facilitated by their local governments' efforts to sustain these services.  However, in many cases, governments do not effectively translate these expectations into actionable plans, leading to unmet needs and dissatisfaction among citizens.  A key challenge here is that governments lack effective tools to bridge the gap between citizens' informal hopes and the official service-level agreements that guide public services.  To address this issue, we have developed an innovative system of 'SmartAssist'.  It consists of three main components: (1) a user-friendly platform for collecting data on citizens' needs and expectations, (2) a sophisticated tool for structuring and formalizing these expectations using formal service-level agreement specifications, and (3) a platform for monitoring progress in meeting these official expectations.  By evaluating the 'SmartAssist' system in a real-world setting, we found it to be a practical solution for translating citizens' informal needs into formal service-level agreements that can be adapted in diverse contexts.  Our study particularly highlights the benefits of flexible agreement specification and monitoring customization in meeting citizens' unmet needs. We've determined that these cross sections exhibit a considerable fluctuation with respect to changes in the top quark mass. On the other hand, using mixed production channels involving top and anti-top quarks, we've observed a considerable flavor dependence that could be uncovered through an adequate analysis. These findings highlight the significance of including substantial flavor effects in top quark pair production calculations, particularly in relevant experimental observations, where mixed production cross sections may provide valuable insights. The use of low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) in infectious disease diagnosis has become a topic of interest, given its potential for reduced radiation exposure and cost savings, despite requiring noise-tolerant image analysis. Accurately diagnosing infectious diseases such as COVID-19 from LDCT scans demands advanced techniques that can distinguish lung abnormalities while withstanding image noise. A Two-stage Time-capsule Network (2T-COVIDnet) has been proposed, which consists of an initial network identifying lung areas from which noise is removed, followed by a capsule network (CAP) detecting COVID-19 from segmented lung images. Results show 2T-COVIDnet effectively increases accuracy when applied to lung cancer and COVID-19 detection tasks, with noise tolerance capabilities demonstrated in COVID-19 detection on noisy CT images. Moreover, its modular design facilitates feature reuse, making the model more efficient and cost-effective compared to other capsule networks. A publicly accessible code repository at https://github.com/wangwangyun/2T-COVIDnet shares the model implementation. Experimental results using CheXpert and COVID19-LDV datasets highlight 2T-COVIDnet's superior performance, outperforming other baselines by CheXpert and matching state-of-the-art performance on COVID19-LDV dataset. Quantitative analysis of model performance reveals a significant p-value of $1.87\times 10^{-5}$ indicating that 2T-COVIDnet's results are not due to chance, as reported by two-tailed t-test comparison of 2T-COVIDnet and CAP on noise-free COVID19-LDV test dataset. Moreover, the model's improved performance is substantial enough to detect COVID-19 from noisy LDCT images with SNR as low as 1. Moreover, the model's error rate indicates that 2T-COVIDnet's results are not due to overfitting, as the model's performance on noise-free and noisy COVID19-LDV test datasets does not differ significantly with p-value of $4.69\times 10^{-8}$. A user study with 10 radiologists further validates the model's capabilities, demonstrating that 2T-COVIDnet's performance outperforms human performance on COVID-19 detection from normal LDCT images with significant p-value of 0.026. A future work suggests extending the model to other infectious diseases such as SARS, MERS, and influenza, which can be achieved by retraining the model on related datasets such as MIMIC-CT. A novel dataset has been developed that maps the utilization of space in the low-earth orbit region. This dataset captures the location and movement of objects within the LEO region over time, providing a comprehensive understanding of spatial usage. The utilization metric used in this study considers both relative and absolute presence of objects/individuals in specific areas. Furthermore, an inference model has been introduced, capable of predicting an entity's presence in a given area at a specified time based solely on its location, velocity, and acceleration. The predictive model effectively uses a one-step forward state prediction and a binary threshold activation function. The developed dataset and models are expected to contribute to a range of applications such as spacecraft trajectory design, debris avoidance, and asteroid mining. These tools can also facilitate the design of LEO architectures for communication networks, including satellite constellations and mesh networks. The dataset is currently available on https://github.com/SpacePrize/dataloading and https://github.com/SpacePrize/inference, with ongoing efforts to include additional features. The codebase utilizes the JAX library for numerical computations and the Pytorch Lightning framework to enhance development efficiency and scalability. The dataset includes training and testing data for multiple entities, with a total of 40 billion simulated time-steps. The training process utilizes the JAX Computation Graph to minimize the training time, achieving a 100% utilization prediction rate on the test set with a sample size of 1 billion time-steps. The inference model is approximately 130 million parameters, with a computation graph depth of 128 and 64 bytes per parameter. The dataset is flexible and can be extended to accommodate additional entities, with potential future developments including data augmentation for robustness, class imbalance correction, and latent representation learning. The code is released under the MIT License to encourage research collaboration. The dataset is currently trained for the LEO region, with potential future expansions to other space regions such as Geo-Orbit and cislunar space. The methods employed in this research can be leveraged to develop novel strategies for data-driven discovery in various domains. The approach is capable of generalization, with results suggesting that it could be applied to presence prediction in other areas such as road usage in urban environments. The approach is also amenable to classification, with results indicating that it could be used to assign labels to unlabeled data. The approach is expected to facilitate the extraction of insights from sensor data, with potential applications in various domains across transportation, energy, and other industries. Mesh coarsening is a process that removes unnecessary details from a mesh, often constructed from CAD models with a high level of detail. To create more simplified meshes, it is necessary to retrospectively adapt the mesh, reducing its complexity. This can be achieved by re-meshing the model using a coarser mesh with lower dimensions. However, altering the mesh topology to change its dimensions is a complex task, especially for topological sensitive applications. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel optimization model that creates order-n coarse meshes directly from the model's CAD representation. This method involves dividing the model into coarser, order-n quadrilateral surfaces using whole-number linear optimization, then creating a mesh based on these surfaces. Both the surface and mesh creation process are influenced by specific constraints. By framing the problem as an optimization with whole-number linear constraints, we ensure the final mesh has a mesh topology with n+1 dimensions. To create meshes with the optimal mesh topology for a specific metric, such as the surface error, we incorporate a constraint that creates meshes with the optimal surface error to a first-order approximation. The sample correlation's probability distribution is examined across various data arrangements, such as the pool, pairs, and within-subgroups. While the distribution is asymptotically normal for any data arrangement, its non-asymptotic moments cannot be calculated analytically and so are approximated through a converging Taylor series. This series is also applicable for non-normal cases. Furthermore, the distribution of the sample correlation in a pool is found to be centered with a level of symmetry, whereas, in pairs and subgroups, bias exists and is calculable. This knowledge is utilized to establish methods for one-sided and powerful tests using the sample correlation. It is also shown that, in a pool, a sample correlation test is a uniform test at optimal strength. Lastly, the corrective actions required for interpreting p-values are established for all data arrangements, along with a discussion of their statistical significance. This study provides the analytical foundation for sample correlation arrangements, similar to similar works for t-statistics or mean estimates. A relevant R package 'corrstats' is developed to verify numerical results. 

For pairs, moment calculations involve a complex hypergeometric series and a Tateyama series.

For subgroups, moment calculations involve the mixed hypergeometric series and the mixed Tateyama series, which were identified as unsolved problems in 2017 and 2019, respectively. 

This work analyzes and solves these problems, further providing special cases for subgroups. 

Using the Tanner-Agnew algorithm, the distribution of the sample correlation for subgroups is found to be centered with a level of symmetry, along with a generalization. 

A Python package 'hypergeometric-ma' is developed to verify numerical results for hypergeometric series and Tateyama series. 

Using the 'taylor-series' package, the Taylor series algorithm is implemented for all data arrangements to calculate the analytical moments of the sample correlation. 

An 'implementation issues' section discusses the difficulties and limitations of the algorithm. 

Finally, the study provides the analytical moments of the sample correlation for all data arrangements, which can be used in statistical tests. 

A relevant R package 'corrstats' is developed to verify numerical results.

We present a novel approach to deriving general relativity and an efficient method for computing post-Newtonian corrections and $S$-matrix elements in various theories of gravity and quantum gravity. A key aspect of our methodology is the use of a background-independent metric that isolates ultraviolet divergences, a technique proven effective in scattering amplitudes calculations. Utilizing dimensional regularization for finite-mass particles calculations is a significant improvement over traditional methods, providing a straightforward solution to loop integrals that has been an open issue for decades. Furthermore, our methodology is adaptable to various gravity theories and quantum gravity scenarios, including loop quantum gravity and string theory, offering a versatile framework for computational work in these fields. We have successfully applied this method to derive an accurate post-Newtonian expansion for the binary black hole effective action, including the third post-Newtonian approximation and the third-order tail-in-inspiral correction. Additionally, our method has been used to compute the one-loop $S$-matrix for graviton exchange and Scattering Amplitudes in Quantum Gravity. Recent advancements have allowed us to calculate the next-order tail-in-inspiral corrections and validate the gravitational wave emission from inspiralling binary black holes through null integration. Moreover, our method has been applied to calculate the one-loop Scattering Amplitudes in Loop Quantum Gravity and String Theory. Future work will involve calculating the next-order corrections to the Scattering Amplitudes and null tests of the gravitational path integral, with a goal of leveraging these calculations to enhance gravitational wave searches and tests of quantum gravity, guided by the principles of effective field theory. Language serves as a distinct characteristic and fundamental means of communication for humans. Mastering language requires dedicated effort and ongoing learning, beginning from an early age. Research into language has gained significant attention from computer science and data science communities, driven by advancements in neural networks and novel methods for analyzing and understanding language in data. A crucial aspect of language research is accessing high-quality text data. Dictionaries, including traditional paper-based and digital Web-based options, serve as essential text data rich in human-created knowledge. Although publicly available dictionaries are limited, particularly in terms of comprehensive coverage and freeness, these resources remain vital for linguistic research and practical applications. As an open-source resource, the LitMind Lexicon can be accessed and utilized by the research community, with plans to continuously update and expand the dataset based on community feedback and updates. LIME is a well-established technique for creating user-friendly approximations of complex machine learning models, explaining how predictions are made. However, research suggests that when applied to the context of recommendations, LIME's localised, instance-specific interpretations can be challenging for users to grasp due to the high number of features involved, such as users and items. To address this, a new method has been developed that enhances LIME's (LIME-RS) outputs by specifically tailoring them to users and showcasing groups of related items, thus making the explanations more compliant with human cognitive capabilities and more suitable for a collaborative filtering setting, such as recommendation systems. The novel approach also introduces a concept of stability - a quantifiable measure of the diversity of interpreted items that can serve as an additional interpretation. The empirical evaluation, conducted using real data from two online recommendation platforms, Hulupic and Last.fm, demonstrates that LIME-RS surpasses the existing state-of-the-art in terms of both precision and a specific cognitive compatibility metric, LIMC, while also being more robust than LIME when applied to recommendations, particularly with regards to the number of features and users' varying levels of expertise. Conceptual space embedding achieves successful results for natural language processing tasks by representing semantic concepts in vector form. Yet, tasks requiring part-of-speech and word sense disambiguation are compromised by the gloss-based approach due to concept drift and local biases in distribution. Regional query prediction methods aim to mitigate this issue by leveraging a set of training examples, but the optimal strategy for selecting these examples remains undefined. This study examines various regional query selection strategies to minimize concept drift and maximize learning resilience. We propose a strategy based on k-center clustering and evaluate its performance against established techniques using multiple sets of concepts. Experimental outcomes across 12 regional query tasks indicate that the k-center strategy surpasses alternative methods by 0.39% in terms of test set accuracy, outperforms methods with larger carbon footprints, and is more resistant to concept drift. Furthermore, the paper introduces a new dataset to aid evaluation and demonstrates the applicability of our findings to real-world contexts via a demonstration example. This research is the first to comprehensively analyze regional query selection strategies, providing valuable insights for practitioners working in related fields. We also present the findings in a manner accessible to both academic and industrial audiences. The research is further documented on our website at https://sites.google.com/view/kcenterregional. Additionally, all data and code are publicly available at https://github.com/alexalexkotov/Regional-Query-Selection. This research ultimately contributes to increased resilience in learning by identifying an effective regional query selection strategy that can be applied to improve outcomes in related tasks. We envision that our research may inspire future work to address additional challenges within the field of NLP. We also plan to explore the extension of our research to tackle more complex problems in related domains. We believe that our research has the potential to make a positive impact in various contexts and contribute valuable knowledge to the NLP community. When exposed to an ionizing radiation field, a substance with charged particles can generate an electric charge due to the interaction with the radiation, which can in turn cause a drag effect on the radiation itself. This phenomenon, known as radiation response drag, is a previously studied effect in which the drag of neutral radiation is increased in proportion to the presence of charged particles in the environment. This study aims to investigate the drag effect on radiation passing through a substance with charged particles when it encounters particle-particle collisions that transfer charge. A first-order linear description of these interactions is developed, leading to an increased drag effect on neutral radiation, with the amount of increase proportional to the number of charged particles involved in collisions. Near Neighbor (NN) and Closest Neighbor (CN) classification methods have gained popularity in machine learning as a form of distance-based classification that doesn't require any pre-processing of the data. However, NN and CN can be flawed when dealing with mixed binary data, as they assign class labels solely based on nearest neighbors without considering relevant distant observations, resulting in poor performance. To overcome this, a new CN statistic has been developed to handle mixed binary data by combining information from both nearest neighbors and distant observations. This CN statistic is based on a mixed binary distance function and utilizes a chi-squared test to determine relevant observations for the classification decision. Additionally, the proposed method eliminates the issues of bias and bias-variance competition by providing several ways to adjust for dimensionality when relevant distant observations are difficult to determine. Simulation studies and real data analyses have demonstrated the proposed method's superior performance compared to traditional NN and CN methods. Our study examines the influence of quantum point and superconducting island interactions on electrical signatures in quantum dots. These interactions can be finely adjusted using a nearby gate, allowing us to identify the relevant processes. Two key processes are identified, involving the coupling of quantum dots to normal and superconducting leads. Lead tunneling rates are quantitatively determined through an in-depth analysis of quantum dot charging dynamics. Various charging events are categorized and their correlations studied, revealing distinct particle tunneling rates to and from the quantum dot. Notably, certain events indicate the simultaneous collapse of two superconducting domains and their corresponding increase in quantum point conductance. This finding is attributed to a visible breakdown of superconductivity and associated changes in quantum point behavior. Furthermore, we observe unique correlations between certain charging events that can be linked to many-body interactions in quantum dot systems. These findings are particularly significant in the context of recent experiments where quantum point and superconducting island coupling were observed without a visible quantum dot. An underlying model of quantum dot confinement has been developed to explain our experimental results. These results are anticipated to facilitate the identification and characterization of quantum code phase transitions in future experiments involving multiple quantum dots. Such advancements may ultimately contribute to a deeper comprehension of quantum tunneling in complex superconducting systems. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the potential for quantum interference in mesoscopic physics to be probed and precisely measured through advanced correlations analysis. Such findings may shed light on the role of quantum fluctuations in driving phase transitions in future quantum information technologies based on superconducting quantum dots. Finally, our findings provide valuable insights into the complex interplay between quantum mechanics, thermodynamics, and tunneling in superconducting quantum electronics, which may also have significant implications for the development of quantum tunneling devices. Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been widely used in image recognition tasks due to their ability to layer increasingly abstract representations. Recent advancements, such as the MixMatch pre-training method, have improved performance by enabling CNNs to generate high-level features from unlabelled data. Nevertheless, this method's reliance on virtual data augmentation poses limitations when applied to small datasets. To address this limitation, this study proposes a pre-training technique called MIMO, which generates pseudo-targets from the mixture of inputs and features to facilitate efficient feature exchange. By utilizing a multi-head self-attention mechanism, MIMO enables the sharing of features among different layers and stages. As a result, this method demonstrates increased resilience and faster training convergence, ultimately achieving a higher accuracy of 82.59% on the CIFAR-10 dataset with only 20 epochs. Furthermore, MIMO produces better feature representations when evaluated on the ImageNet dataset, achieving a significant accuracy of 88.53% with 80 epochs. Notably, this method produces superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, such as pre-trained CNNs, semi-supervised learning techniques, and self-supervised learning methods. MIMO's performance can be further enhanced by fine-tuning the model with a small labelled dataset, showcasing its potential to outperform baseline methods by 10.6% on the CIFAR-100 dataset with only 10 extra labelled images. The effectiveness of a compensation method for an industrial robot's position tracking error is evaluated, and its ability to enhance stability is assessed, utilizing a simplified control approach in a one-degree-of-freedom planar system over a mid-range trajectory. Two feedback systems are compared: one relying on a measure of actuator force, which can detect but not prevent position tracking errors, and another using a measure of system rigidity, which can not only detect but also mitigate such errors. Experimental data indicates that the position tracking error is reduced from 2.64% to 0.66% when employing the new approach, resulting in a corresponding decrease in the actuator's overshoot from 12.89% to 2.98%. Moreover, the novel method allows for position tracking accuracy comparable to that of high-end robots with sophisticated sensors within an affordable framework. It is worth noting, however, that in scenarios requiring precise positioning, position feedback remains indispensable, and this method is intended for applications where position feedback is unfeasible or prohibitively expensive to obtain. The source code for the robot controller has been made publicly available on GitHub. The research highlights the importance of employing multiple system parameters for designing control strategies, particularly when dealing with underdamped systems prone to overshooting, a parameter-free approach having minimal practical applications. The study also underscores the value of characterizing system dynamics through sensory observation of secondary parameters rather than relying solely on performance metrics. Finally, it demonstrates that positioning accuracy comparable to that of high-end robots can be achieved with a relatively simple addition of secondary parameters in the control loop.
