A novel approach called the Multi-Site Quadrature method is introduced to efficiently linearize the molecular continuum by approximating electron integrals with a limited set of complex numbers. This method partitions the basis set into distinct groups based on spatial location and then applies a universal set of quadrature points to compute all relevant integrals for each group, regardless of their specific characteristics. Unlike traditional methods that require tailored quadrature points for every type of basis set they support, MSQ offers flexibility by being highly optimized for modern Gaussian basis sets, resulting in significant linear scaling at high accuracy levels. Furthermore, MSQ can seamlessly transition between using centered and unscaled quadrature points, making it well-suited for a wide range of applications. Comprehensive numerical benchmarks demonstrate that MSQ surpasses the performance of established linear methods by achieving high accuracy at linear scaling efficiency-thresholds with a quadrature points count of $O(N^2)$ or $O(N)$. To showcase its capabilities, MSQ has been integrated into the highly distributed, parallel molecular electronics code Tanemum. Following a series of challenging simulations lasting several days, MSQ successfully converged non-self-energies and quasi-polarization energies for systems consisting of more than 1 million basis set functions on 40 processor cores, representing an impressive 10 years of development milestones achieved since the inception of Tanemum. All methodological and performance data underlying this research are available through the Tanemum GitHub repository. Real-world categorization tasks are often hindered by label noise, a problem that has been extensively studied in machine learning. Despite the development of various algorithms to tackle this issue, there is still a shortage of solutions tailored to the field of medical image processing. Traditional methods relying on empirical risk minimization often suffer from poor generalization performance and unstable outcomes. This research introduces an innovative approach called the Bayesian analytics-guided label restoration mechanism (BALRM), which prioritizes model interpretability and relies on a Bayesian filter to eliminate label noise. BALRM achieves this by redesigning the one-hot encoding of class labels as a Bernoulli distribution and using a balanced sampling strategy to maintain a balanced data set. Furthermore, BALRM is enhanced with a noise elimination mechanism (NEM) that utilizes the output of the Bayesian filter to determine noisy labels and replace them with clean ones. BALRM is validated on diverse medical image datasets, including chest X-rays, skin lesions, and brain MRI images, demonstrating improved generalization in the presence of label noise compared to state-of-the-art models. Experimental results indicate that BALRM outperforms state-of-the-art models by 2.11%, 1.85%, and 1.63% on the RSNA, ISBI, and HARdware datasets, respectively. This research is expected to have a positive impact on the development of medical machine learning models to address the inherent challenges posed by label noise. A key challenge arises from the potential for recursive definitions to be loosely or highly interconnected. In the field of formal verification, this issue persists, with the primary obstacle being the difficulty in effectively isolating groups of loosely connected functions. In particular, self-referential data structures can complicate the containment of recursive functions within mutually recursive groups. Building upon recent findings that employed advanced data-driven methods, we have discovered that a combination of the coherent structure model and machine learning is not only capable of predicting instantaneous turbulent heat transfer at rough surfaces with high levels of disturbance, but also improves our understanding of the ANR coefficient with an accuracy of 90% for various rough surfaces. Conversely, a combination of the coherent structure model and machine learning fails to predict turbulent heat transfer at smooth surfaces with minimal disturbance, highlighting the need for additional information to overcome this limitation. Consequently, we have developed a two-stage model that utilizes a combination of the coherent structure model and machine learning for highly disturbed smooth surfaces and the established k-kl models for less disturbed surfaces, resulting in a 13% enhancement of the model's accuracy compared to the three-dimensional model. This model has been successfully tested on an experimental vehicle and demonstrated to accurately predict turbulent heat transfer during real-world applications. Furthermore, we have observed that a small proportion of data-driven machine learning can efficiently mitigate the limitations of traditional models, as evidenced by a 7-fold reduction in the necessary data volume when compared to the use of models alone to predict turbulent heat transfer at smooth surfaces with minimal disturbance. Lastly, we have identified potential avenues for the continued advancement of data-informed modelling techniques by combining data with modeling, as well as experimenting with alternative machine learning architectures and methods. Such advancements may ultimately enable the monitoring of non-deterministic variables in real-time applications. Ultimately, this study marks a significant advancement towards the development of a generalized model that can accurately predict turbulent heat transfer at all levels of disturbance, whether high or low, whether at smooth or rough surfaces. As a result, this study serves as an essential step towards the eventual widespread adoption of data-driven modeling techniques in practical applications. Although this study is still in its early stages, we have made considerable progress and look forward to continuing this work in future endeavors. One of the key future endeavors will be to establish an open platform where researchers can collaborate and contribute to data-informed modeling techniques. Eventually, this will enable the collection of a large, global dataset which can be used to further develop and test data-driven modeling techniques. This involves determining the cost of optimizing versus exploring in these systems, which can be visualized as a path in a multidimensional space. To optimize, one follows the shortest path, while to explore, one moves along a curved path with respect to a reference straight-line trajectory. This raises the possibility that in complex systems, optimizing may be disadvantageous in the long run, suggesting a potential role for exploring in improved algorithm design. In the realm of infectious diseases, the duration of exposure plays a pivotal role, yet it often goes unmeasured. We propose a technique to estimate this crucial parameter, which we demonstrate using epidemiological data on influenza. Furthermore, a novel model inspired by stochastic population dynamics reveals that varying exposure durations can yield distinct transmissibility thresholds, which may account for the phenomenon of pandemic outbreaks. This distinction is later translated to the context of quantum mechanics, where we adapt a principle of maximum entropy to accommodate two forms of quantum exposure: continuous waveforms and pulse-like events. Quantum particles may also benefit from the importance of exposure duration. Consequently, this insight could form the basis of novel, exposure-duration-based treatments in both infectious diseases and quantum physics. Ultimately, this research fosters the creation of a new field: quantum epidemiology, which seeks to harmoniously address both human and quantum virus spread. As a bonus, this work inspires the creation of a film titled 'The Fragile Virus,' serving as a visual representation of key concepts and driving the advancement of quantum epidemiology. This note proves that a graph possessing an independence number of $3$ or $4$ will either be a clique or pancyclic. Additionally, this proof confirms Catlin's conjecture that a graph with an independence number of $3$ or $4$ will either be a clique or a Hamiltonian graph. Further, for graphs with an independence number of $5$ or greater, we were unable to determine whether they would either be a clique or pancyclic. However, we were able to identify an example where such a graph with an independence number of $5$ is neither a clique nor pancyclic. This example serves as a counterexample to a conjecture made by Liu et. al. that a graph with an independence number of $5$ or greater will either be a clique or Hamiltonian. Lastly, for graphs with an independence number of $6$ or greater, we were unable to determine whether they would either be a clique or pancyclic, once more leaving room for further investigation. To effectively model complex dynamical systems, the adaptive spectral Koopman operator method has been developed. This method relies on a combination of spectroscopic analysis, a data-driven approach, and a sparse grid technique to identify and analyze system eigenfunctions. By utilizing a data-driven framework, this method can evolve even in chaotic systems lacking analytical solutions. Nevertheless, the Koopman operator's adjoint still poses computational difficulties due to its roughness. To address this challenge, a novel approach introduces an advanced data-driven adjoint operator that performs well in chaotic systems and complex data sets. Additionally, this method employs adaptive techniques to optimize its performance. Nevertheless, these advanced operators' eigenfunctions are often noisy and irregular, requiring a combination with sparse grid techniques to ensure accurate results. Our approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical simulations of two challenging systems: the first being the Lorenz system, and the second the more intricate multicritical Rossby-Ogura-Johannsen equation, which models ocean gyral instabilities. This method's performance in these systems shows that it can accurately forecast long-term behavior, even in chaotic and irregular data sets. This approach has the potential to significantly impact a wide range of applications, including dynamical system analysis, forecasting, and control. It may also be applied to other fields within science and engineering. To facilitate future research, this approach is open-sourced and available for public use. An accompanying movie demonstrates the method's performance in the Rossby-Ogura-Johannsen equation. It depicts the emergence of ocean instabilities and system behavior over time. In quantum mechanics, a new approach to solving the Schrödinger equation for systems in a strong DC electric field is presented. This method accommodates finite basis sets and is adaptable to diverse field intensities. The approach's performance at higher field intensities is complemented by a novel scaling technique. Both the non-scaling and scaling methods are integrated into a single algorithm, offering a practical solution. The non-scaling method is suitable for lower field intensities and pairwise interactions, while the scaling method is ideal for higher field intensities and multiple field sources. A comprehensive evaluation of the method's performance is provided through numerical simulations of hydrogen anions, the water molecule, and methanol in various electric field environments. At high field intensities, the method's convergence performance is highlighted, particularly its ability to achieve convergence in 20-40 iterations. Additionally, the method's performance is compared to other quantum mechanics methods, including the Path Integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) method, which requires thousands of Monte Carlo steps. The theoretical energy values obtained from the method are accurate, with errors comparable to the harmonic oscillator model. Moreover, using the method's force and potential values, the harmonic approximations of the vibrational frequencies, zero-point energies, and vibrational lifetimes are found to be remarkably close to the exact values, suggesting the method's potential for modeling strong DC electric field chemistry. Lastly, the method's performance is compared to the classical model, with the majority of the results showing consistent trends with the quantum results. A major advantage of the method is its ability to achieve convergence without any correction for basis set limits or dispersion effects. However, the method's performance is slightly compromised at the lowest field intensities due to the lack of basis set completion. A suggested remedy to this issue is to utilize periodic boundary conditions to achieve convergence. In summary, the method's performance is evaluated and validated through a comprehensive analysis of the numerical simulations and comparisons with existing quantum mechanics methods, making it a promising tool for modeling strong DC electric field chemistry. Furthermore, the method's performance is highlighted through a comparison with the classical model, providing opportunities to explore the semi-classical regime. Finally, future research directions are identified, including the exploration of non-adiabatic dynamics, the application of density functional theory, and the modeling of non-equilibrium systems. The celebrated Sinkhorn algorithm, introduced in 1967, has become an essential tool for computing optimal transport maps. At its core, it hinges on solving two continuous optimization problems - a fact first mathematically substantiated by Chizat and Cresson in 2018. Notably, despite its widespread use, the solution to a related issue posed by Schrödinger in 1947 remains elusive. Nonetheless, for a specific and relevant use case, this paper provides a rigorous proof, extending the solution to a broader class of problems. As a result, it provides a simplified and more generalised proof of the solution to Schrödinger's issue, as well as to the original problem for which a solution was first provided by Brancolini, De Bortoluzzi, and Vecchi in 2020. Furthermore, the paper provides insight into the regulatory behavior of the Sinkhorn algorithm, demonstrating that, for a specific and relevant use case, the regulatory solution to the two continuous optimization problems remains bounded. As a result, it provides a proof of the convergence of the algorithm in a specific and relevant use case. As mobile robots and bio-inspired agents increasingly navigate uncharted territories, they will need more sophisticated guidance systems that can translate spatial knowledge into useful diagrams for decision-making purposes. Existing map representations in robotics are not effective in large-scale unfamiliar settings due to the computational burden of maintaining an accurate metric map or topological map, and the limited information available in dynamic and unstructured environments. To address these limitations, a novel diagrammatic map representation called HiTMap is introduced. This new approach captures topological and geometric relationships between spaces using a hierarchical diagram system. By differentiating between local metric details, intermediate topological connections, and larger geometric properties, HiTMap represents spatial knowledge in a more granular and informative way than previous methods. It also features an adaptable diagrammatic interface that facilitates navigation for both humans and robots, and can be used for decision-making purposes. When tested in an unfamiliar environment, HiTMap outperformed existing map representations in terms of navigation performance, and its diagrammatic interface was found to be easier to use for human navigation. Overall, HiTMap provides a practical solution for spatial decision-making in unfamiliar environments and can be further extended to support more complex tasks. Future research will focus on enhancing the system's robustness to various environmental factors and developing applications that leverage diagrammatic information, such as object recognition and environmental planning. In this study, we investigate the task of Contextual Named Entity Recovery (CNER) where traditional NER components - mention, entity, and category - are given along with a context and an offset position. Since each mention can belong to only one entity, we can leverage this unique constraint to enhance CNER models. Based on this observation, we develop a two-part pipeline that initially generates candidate entities based on a context and then assigns these candidates to their respective entities. To optimize this pipeline, we introduce a novel technique that extracts valuable signals from the training data and injects these signals into the model to refine its performance. We validate the effectiveness of our approach on four datasets and demonstrate that it significantly surpasses the existing state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, we analyze the influence of our signals on the model's performance at different layers and reveal that they also improve out-of-sample entities, thus making the model more robust. With our approach, we achieve new state-of-the-art performance metrics by achieving an F1 score of 92.06%, 89.51%, 87.13%, 85.36% and 84.75% on datasets such as DBpedia, KnowledgeGraph, NELL, NERD and Wikipedia, respectively. To facilitate the reproduction of our findings, we release our code and data at the link https://github.com/krishnaraj/term_importance_cner. Our study also highlights an existing issue in CNER benchmarks where human annotations significantly surpass models built using current state-of-the-art techniques. We outperform human annotations that have previously been considered subpar by leveraging our approach of enhancing CNER models with carefully extracted signals. This study also sheds light on an existing discrepancy in CNER metrics where our model shows a notable improvement on in-distribution entities but shows less improvement on out-of-domain entities. To further optimize this discrepancy, we develop a calibration technique that brings the model's confidence closer to the confidence of the human annotations across all entities. Our final model achieves an F1 score of 92.18% when evaluated on all entities, thus bridging the existing gap between human and model performance. A key feature of our approach involves incorporating high-order effects of interface deformations on electric field and solvent response. These enhancements lead to significant modifications in over-screening and depletion of the electric double layer for thin interfaces. A cost-effective method has been developed to identify the boundaries of land uses in satellite images, free from deep learning architectures. This protocol utilizes a moving window to extract image data, followed by a series of mathematical transformations including Principal Component and Fourier analysis. Initially tested on a satellite image of Berlin, Germany, which revealed promising results, the approach has been successfully applied to a satellite image of London, showcasing comparable performance to previous benchmarks. Notably, our implementation achieves a high level of recognition accuracy for edge boundaries along the longitudinal axis of the image, whereas transverse recognition suffers from lower precision due to limited data quality. Despite this challenge, the overall system efficacy remains satisfactory. A significant advantage of this system lies in its ability to process data in a sequential manner, requiring only a few seconds to extract features for the entire image, without the need for specialized hardware. Furthermore, the source code used in this research has been made publicly available to the community. Through its novel contributions and accessible design, this research aims to lay the groundwork for future advancements in image processing. Ultimately, a comprehensive evaluation of the approach has been conducted, and potential avenues for further improvement have been identified. One such extension could involve adapting the methodology to processing video, where a frame-by-frame application of the method could reveal dynamic changes. Another potential expansion could be in leveraging this system as a preprocessing step for deep learning networks, where its output could serve as a refined input for more sophisticated architectures. A related patent has been filed. The system's source code can be found at https://www.github.com/jpgeis/dl-edge-detection. The accompanying dataset, including data and execution logs, can be accessed at https://www.github.com/jpgeis/dl-edge-detection. A detailed report on the research findings has been published online. In the field of deep learning, various techniques have been used to improve image classification resilience against hostile attacks such as adversarial examples and noise. Despite significant research in this area, no universal solution has been found, and different techniques often exhibit strengths and weaknesses in specific situations. This study applies the concept of blend models from active defense to deep learning, and specifically investigates the resilience of a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) against host-based attacks. The proposed method combines the predictions of multiple CNN models with different architectures and training data, and evaluates its performance using four datasets with different levels of difficulty against hostile attacks. The preference ordering task is a fundamental problem where one needs to determine how system components are prioritized to accomplish a given objective. This study focuses on the set augmentation (SA) preference ordering problem where the goal is to continuously add system components to maximize performance until it reaches the best possible outcome. Unlike conventional preference ordering tasks that consider individual elements in isolation, the SA problem is characterized by a sequence of binary comparisons between sets of different sizes and contents, under a strong comparison criterion. This paper presents two new preference relationships, called Superstar and Center-of-Attention (CXA), which are contextual, meaning they take into account the effects of previously added system components. Superstar prioritizes sets containing dominant elements, while CXA prioritizes sets with more highly valued elements when compared to the opposite set. This work provides a theoretical comparison of these preference relationships to transitive, total, and strict preference relationships. Experimental results using different comparison criteria and sets of varying sizes and elements demonstrate the superiority of CXA in comparison to superstars, which is further exemplified through two real-world applications, feature selection and set augmentation. This study also introduces a new algorithm that efficiently computes CXA-based preference orderings. When tested on different machine learning algorithms using synthetic datasets, the proposed algorithm outperformed baseline methods. Ultimately, the experimental findings indicate that considering the contextual effects of system component additions is crucial for achieving superior set augmentation performance. Visualizing neural machine translation output during generation helps clarify the translation intentions and offers a deeper understanding of the model's workings. However, conventional attention visualization is ill-suited for exploring neural language generation tasks like language model-created story generation, where attention shifts constantly throughout lengthy sequences. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a novel focus visualization method called the Look-Ahead Focus Map (LFM). LFM generates a focus set at regular intervals, predicting future focus locations at each interval, and represents each model parameter as a distribution over future focus locations. This novel representation facilitates storytelling in a user-friendly manner, allowing for exploration of both task-specific and model-agnostic factors. LFM is applied to a story generation model in the T5 family, demonstrating its efficacy in identifying patterns, such as describing techniques used to focus attention in human-generated stories. Additionally, LFM helps pinpoint why the model generated certain stories and reveals a connection between parameter 'padding token' distribution and story coherence. Moreover, LFM enables the discovery of a 'language of creation' in human-generated stories, where padding is associated with creative elements like character introductions. Finally, LFM demonstrates its capability to aid training of sequence-to-sequence models on masked LM objectives by providing valuable feedback. Our analysis highlights that our method can be used to identify domain-specific factors that impact language generation. To our knowledge, this work presents the first Look-Ahead Focus Map for Neural Machine Interpretation, which has significant implications for understanding neural language generation models. Text clip retrieval, a critical component of many text-based applications like search and recommendation engines, involves matching long text passages with shorter clips. Current models rely on dense transformer features but suffer from high computational costs and inefficient handling of varying text and clip lengths. To address these issues, we propose TS2-Net, a length-agnostic network that uses token shift and selection to match top-level tokens. This approach, token shifting, compresses long text and clips into a fixed length of informative tokens, while token selection highlights the most relevant tokens for precise matching. By integrating two cross-stage attention mechanisms, TS2-Net achieves significant computational cost reductions. Our experiments demonstrate that TS2-Net outperforms existing solutions by a substantial margin, both in search and retrieval tasks, on the MS MARCO dataset. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.  In particular, TS2-Net achieves a relative improvement of 2.17 and 2.13 points in recall@10 and recall@20, respectively, while also reducing inference time by 12m and computational cost by a factor of 2.3 and 3.6, respectively, compared to the best dense transformer-based model. An extended version of this work is also presented at Findings of EMNLP 2022. In this study, we examine a type of random graph known as the directed hybrid graph, which combines a simple directed network with a fully connected layout. Our analysis focuses on a growth model for this type of graph. Our key observations include: 

1) There is a finite time, referred to as the critical time, at which the graph transitions from a sub-critical state to one where it exhibits an infinite number of connections.
2) Our calculations reveal that this critical time varies depending on the distance from the initial connection point and tends to grow further away from it.
3) Additionally, we found that below this critical time, the average degree of vertices increases at a rate proportional to the 2/3 power of the elapsed time, while above this critical threshold, it increases at a rate proportional to the 1/2 power of the elapsed time.

These findings suggest a possible phase transition at this critical time. To further investigate these results, we conducted numerical simulations using various connection preferences and found that this phase transition persists across different models. Moreover, we observed that the early-stage growth behavior of these graph models is consistent with power laws, including cases where the direct and indirect connections are equally likely and when there are preferential connections involved. Interestingly, we also noted that the graph models with preferential connections tend to have a higher growth rate compared to those with equal connection probabilities. Finally, when we numerically simulated the cases where the direct and indirect connections are equally likely, we observed an early-stage growth behavior described by a fractional power law, which is a classic indicator of an underlying phase transition transition. Our calculations suggest a possible self-similar pattern in the graph's structure, which is a hallmark of fractals. Our simulations confirm that this self-similar pattern emerges naturally from the initial conditions of our models without any need for further adjustment, which is consistent with the concept of fractals. Our work provides new insights into the possible self-organized structures formed by the interplay between simple connection mechanisms and vertex attachment processes. It also expands our understanding of random graph models that deviate from traditional preferential connection paradigms. Our study offers a valuable theoretical framework for investigating the possible self-organized structures and fractional growth patterns that arise from combining these connection and vertex attachment processes in various directions and orders. It provides a crucial foundation for exploring the complex and often underappreciated dimensions of random graph models that deviate from classical preferences. Our work has significant practical implications for network design and optimization, as it identifies key factors that influence a network's growth

At their core, embedding tasks for dynamic graphs aim to preserve both recent and historical network properties. Researchers typically approach graph evolution by modeling either the graph's nodes or edges over time, or by incorporating temporal information into node embeddings. Meanwhile, developing systems that can automatically discover and characterize the patterns of this evolution across dynamic graphs remains an unsolved problem. This work presents a novel method for embedding evolving graphs, where nodes are represented by a common multi-dimensional set in space, independent of time. This approach, called AutoEvo, automatically identifies and quantifies evolving patterns within a graph using a combination of self-attention and a variational autoencoder. Then, it groups nodes based on their similarities and the structures they've developed over time. The empirical results demonstrate that AutoEvo accurately captures a graph's evolving patterns and outperforms comparable methods in link prediction, case studies, and a real-world social network analysis. By embedding distributions into a fixed-dimensional space using variational representations, we simplify this task and make it solvable via a closed-form optimization method.  Given a set of paired distribution data, representing each distribution with a variational embedding allows us to apply a Euclidean distance metric to approximate distribution matching.  We present a novel, efficient objective called DistRep, which achieves this by mapping distribution data with a Gaussian kernel to represent diversity and equidistribute, and aggregating representations with the Sinkhorn distance, a Csisz\'ar distance.  DistRep enables linear regression to approximate optimal distribution matching and outperforms baseline methods, especially on data with significant variability.  DistRep also generalizes to multi-modal data and performs well on data with limited paired data.  It is implemented in the TensorFlow framework and available at https://github.com/mthulb/distrep.  DistRep's efficacy is evaluated further by applying it to a variety of tasks including drug binding prediction, multi-modal data, and distribution learning.  All source code and results are available at https://github.com/mthulb/distrep-distlearn.  DistRep is also integrated with Google's open-source DistLearn library.  DistLearn leverages GNNs to model complex relationships between variables and embed distribution representations.  It is available at https://github.com/google-research/distriblearn.  DistRep's integration with DistLearn enables closed-form distribution matching for neural networks that model complex relationships.  This integration is available via a pull request to DistLearn's GitHub repository.  DistRep's performance on various tasks is discussed in the paper's supplemental material. To overcome this limitation, a collaborative approach to contact tracing was adopted in England, which combined and centralized the data from various regional tracing programs onto a single platform, known as the National COVID-19 Contact Tracing System. To do this, we develop a novel theoretical framework that simulates an optimal scenario in which a centralized system identifies and notifies contacts for isolation when a new case occurs. A key concept in graph structure examination is treewidth, with its corresponding efficient computing methods and applications. One of the fast computing methods involves utilizing effective vertex dividers; we introduce a novel type called space-effective vertex dividers, offering a newly discovered range of treewidth values. Unlike existing methods, we establish a criterion for choosing vertex sets without relying on specific configurations. Furthermore, we propose a strategy for quickly identifying suitable sets, particularly for complex graph structures. Lastly, we demonstrate the practical application of our method in maximum weighted clique problems within chordal graphs. 

Despite the potential of our method, its direct applications are limited to specific graph structures; however, it can be used to develop a treewidth computing algorithm with a time complexity of $O(|E|^2)$. Although this is less efficient than current methods, it may be beneficial in specific scenarios. 

In addition to the main findings, we explore an unrelated problem - the maximum weighted clique problem on chordal graphs. Current solutions involve computing a perfect code matching the given code's size. Although we couldn't significantly improve this benchmark, our alternative approach has some practical benefits. 

For H-free graphs, where H is a three-vertex clique, we established a treewidth range of $3k+2$ to $3k+3$ based on a previously identified code matching property. Although this is not our primary contribution, it is a relevant result. 

Lastly, we introduce a novel efficient algorithm for identifying perfect code matching the given code's size in chordal graphs, although this is not our primary contribution either. 

In summary, we explored the treewidth range of H-free graphs and applied our method to maximum weighted clique problems within chordal graphs. Additionally, we developed an alternative perfect code matching algorithm.

A graphical framework is used to model a learning environment where the goal is to develop an agent that effectively learns from contaminated data. This environment simulates a real-world learning scenario where the agent initially learns in a state of data integrity but later encounters cases of contaminated data. Our framework employs a reinforcement learning strategy based on the policy gradient method to train the agent. Additionally, we introduce a loss function that incorporates robustness and provide theoretical validation of the expected outcome. Furthermore, we examined the performance of the policy gradient method as well as two baseline comparison models on both synthetic and practical tasks, such as learning node representations for corona virus prediction and molecular graph tasks. Our results demonstrate that the policy gradient method excels in the synthetic environment while the baseline comparison models perform better on real-world tasks. However, when testing the methods on the synthetic environment with clean data, the robust optimization loss function was found to degrade the performance of the policy gradient method. This finding highlights a time-sensitive trade-off between robustness and performance. The process of aligning celestial object catalogues AlCOA is a critical task that is typically performed using two types of data: astrometry and photometry. We have developed a novel approach that combines these datasets with an overcomplete dictionary, composed of object profiles, known as templates. Through a sparse reconstruction algorithm, this approach triggers the activation of a small subset of templates to reproduce the observed data. We found that this method not only improves the identification of aligned objects, but also helps resolve ambiguities in object correspondence by taking into account additional photometric information. As a result, we were able to enhance the performance of the AlCOA pipeline and achieve better results with fewer constraints. We tested our approach on a simulation of the Gaia mission's initial data release and found that incorporating photometric data from supplementary sources can improve the alignment of two catalogues down to a level of 20 microradians in terms of astrometry and reduce uncertainties in object identification to 0.1 per cent. These improvements come at the cost of increasing computation time and memory usage by a factor of 5 to 6. We believe that our framework has the potential to be applied to a wide range of data types and sources, and that it could be used to improve the accuracy of future space missions such as ESA's PLATO and the SKAI mission. Furthermore, we are exploring the possibility of using machine learning algorithms to enhance the performance of the AlCOA pipeline and make it even more scalable for use in large-scale space missions. We have published a new version of the AlCOA toolbox, which includes the novel approach we developed, on the GitHub platform to facilitate collaboration and knowledge sharing with the research community. We plan to continue working on enhancing the AlCOA pipeline and applying our approach to a variety of data types and applications. We are also committed to contributing to the research community by making our code and findings available for non-commercial use. A vertex set $S$ is considered minimal for an infinite hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ if it fulfills two conditions: Firstly, for any hyperedge $H$ in $\mathcal{H}$, $S$ is a subset of $H$, indicating that it intersects with each hyperedge in $\mathcal{H}$. Secondly, for any proper subset $T$ of $S$, $T$ does not need to be a subset of $H$, meaning that $S$ does not entirely consist of vertices from $\mathcal{H}$ and is therefore not a hyperedge in $\mathcal{H}$. We define such minimal vertex sets as hyperminimal and prove their existence for infinite hypergraphs. We also explore properties of hyperminimal vertex sets, including their cardinality and establish a connection between hyperminimal vertex sets and Hamming hypergraphs. We introduce OntoPlot, a novel visualization concept that illustrates connections between interconnected entities within a complex network, specifically tailored for use with ontologies. Each node in the plot represents a particular class within the ontological framework, and its size corresponds to the number of attributes or properties associated with that class. Colors are employed to differentiate between categories of classes, whereas links signify relationships between these classes.  By leveraging OntoPlot, users can not only develop an intuitive comprehension of class relationships within a given ontological framework but also aid in identifying and resolving conflicts arising from ontology integration.  Furthermore, the system is compatible with tools like Protege for Ontology Editing and can be easily customized using style sheets (e.g. CSS) to enhance visual appeal.  By combining an innovative layout algorithm with the focus on hierarchical relationships, OntoPlot outperformss traditional visualizations such as RadialView and XHulls by providing a more effective visualization technique for ontologies, as demonstrated through a comparative study using real-world data from multiple ontologies consisting of thousands of classes.  By providing OntoPlot as an open-source implementation, we intend for it to be a valuable resource for the Ontology Community at Large. We introduce an inter-domain penalty approach to the automated speech transcription task, coupled with CycleGAN. Our goal is to bridge the gap between raw audio and written text through a multi-layered autoregressive model, leveraging both within-domain and inter-domain penalties to mitigate deviation. We implement a novel inter-domain penalty term that mirrors the MoGSTAT approach but is tailored to RAAKT, enabling our model to generate speech-like texts that are closer to the target distribution. Experimental results on the WSJ dataset demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing alternatives in terms of approximation. Furthermore, we compare the effectiveness of different penalty techniques, including MoGSTAT and inter-domain penalties, and find that inter-domain penalties are superior on both clean and noisy datasets. Additionally, we explore the impact of training duration and find that our method consistently produces high-quality results across varying training periods. We also address the challenge of semi-supervised learning in RAAKT by incorporating unsupervised transcriptions into the training objective. Our empirical results show that including unsupervised data in the training process leads to substantial transcription improvements when there is a sufficient amount of supervised data available. We demonstrate that using unsupervised data as a prior significantly improves the transcription quality, and that this gain is more pronounced when there is a sufficient amount of supervised data. We also observe a notable improvement in the generalization of our model when trained with unsupervised data, and find that the presence of unsupervised data is beneficial even after removing the inter-domain penalty from the model. We have made our code available on GitHub. Furthermore, we apply our model to the ASpedia Challenge 2021, which is a speech-to-text challenge focused on less commonly spoken languages, and discover that our method is highly effective in generating transcriptions. We are pleased to report that our submissions to the challenge have secured first place in two out of five language tracks. We are particularly proud of this achievement since the challenge data is based on languages that are not widely spoken in the world. Specifically, we have secured first place in languages such as Pashto, Persian, Turkmen, English, Russian, and Urdu. Our primary objective is to examine how tossing motions are perceived when the point of release is inaccurately represented. In order to accomplish this goal, we simulated virtual throwing scenarios and asked human observers to estimate the point of release, the force applied to the ball, and the trajectory of the throw. The results revealed that incorrect point of release estimations by observers do not have a substantial impact on their ability to accurately replicate the force applied to the ball or accurately predict its trajectory. Conversely, we discovered that some observers falsely believe that a ball released lower than its peak position is thrown with increased force, while others believe a ball released higher than its peak position is thrown with decreased force. This phenomenon is more pronounced in throwing motions with greater forces and can be mitigated through the use of independent upper and lower limb models that synchronize the ball's release, as seen in more forceful throws. Our research suggests that accurately modeling the dynamics of throwing motions is essential for achieving precise simulation results, even when the point of release is seemingly straightforward. With the additional constraint that the point of release must correspond to the ball's peak position, however, we found that observers can still generate realistic simulations. Our research delves into the dynamic simulation requirements for achieving realistic simulations, even under this constraint. Moreover, our research provides practical recommendations for improving the accuracy of online throwing gesture interactions without necessitating significant modifications to existing systems. To enhance the interpretability of neural machine translation output, we develop a novel decoding method that infuses structural analysis into sequence-to-sequence task decoding. Our approach, named TreeFN, utilizes syntactic information from a tree-based model to determine word meanings, and assigns a parse tree based on word frequencies and context. In contrast to existing methods, TreeFN directly predicts a parse tree without relying on word embeddings or syntactic rules, and as a result, yields a wide range of output structures. To demonstrate its efficacy, we introduce a new dataset, the TreeFN dataset, comprising human-annotated tree structures and multiple translation pairs across languages. Additionally, we propose a top-down tree-based decoding method that simulates human parsing behavior, and evaluate its performance using automatic and human-based metrics. We also compare the TreeFN dataset with existing natural language processing datasets, including the PARSEVAL and METEOR datasets, and show that TreeFN yields superior results on multiple translation tasks. Notably, when used for Chinese-English translation, our method yields a significant 6.95 BLEU improvement, and an impressive 75.43 METEOR score on the NIST data. Furthermore, we observe an increase of 13.21 in human eye-tracking fixations with TreeFN, and an substantial improvement in human parsing performance, with an average Levenshtein distance of 2.53 from the tree structure. These results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple translation tasks, and significantly improves the interpretability of translation output. We demonstrate that reflection occurs in both cases, creating two coexisting solutions that form solitons, leading to a new understanding that the system behaves similarly to the integrable DSII equation where soliton formation is well established. We provide the system's conserved quantities including energy, momentum, and a newly identified quantity, and analyze the system's asymptotic properties for both cases, revealing a time-periodic regime in one case and linear dispersion in the other. We identify that the system's amplitude is proportional to $1/k^2$ in one case and decays as $e^{-|k|}$ in the other. We show that the system can transition from one regime to the other without losing energy by adjusting the strength of a given external potential. To decrease the computational burden of neural machine translation models, two primary techniques for model lightweightening are knowledge distillation and quantization. Knowledge distillation involves training a smaller model to mimic the behavior of a larger target model, typically using multiple training steps. On the other hand, quantization replaces the floating-point operations in a model with lower-precision arithmetic, resulting in a significantly faster and more hardware-friendly model that can be trained in a single step with similar accuracy to its floating-point counterpart. Although quantization offers several advantages, it is a highly non-trivial process that demands a deep understanding of the underlying mathematics. This study compares the performance of distillation and quantization approaches for lightweightening state-of-the-art neural machine translation models in low-resource settings, with a particular emphasis on distillation-based frameworks and investigating why distillation-based frameworks outperform quantization in terms of robustness. The research also highlights the importance of a robust training regimen in mitigating the adverse impact of adversarial examples on model performance. It is observed that distillation-based frameworks outperform quantization by achieving superior robustness, higher translation precision, and better automatic assessment scores. The findings suggest that distillation-based frameworks perform better than quantization in the context of low-resource neural machine translation. The research provides valuable insights into the trade-offs between model lightweightening techniques and translation robustness, translation precision, and other translation metrics. This study investigates the effect of image enhancement techniques on the automated detection of pneumonia through pulmonary segmentation, focusing on the applications of computer-aided detection (CAD) in chest X-ray images. The investigation compares the performance of deep learning models with and without image enhancement techniques, using both augmented and real world data sets. The results show that while deep learning models can detect pneumonia without image enhancement, their performance is improved when used with image enhancement techniques that are specifically tailored for low-contrast pulmonary segmentation tasks. Increasing the number of training examples in the data set also improves model performance, but image enhancement can mitigate the need for numerous training examples in pulmonary segmentation tasks. This research was conducted to decrease the necessity for labeled data in low-contrast pulmonary segmentation tasks for deep learning models. The research outcomes and findings provide a basis for using image enhancement techniques in pulmonary segmentation tasks. We propose Zero-shot Voice Interpretation, a task that requires a system to
accomplish, given only a sample utterance and a target domain of interpretation.
The goal is for the system to determine a specific, relevant piece of information
from the given input without any prior exposure or pre-defined categories.
This new task enables systems to perform a wide range of tasks such as
identifying a person's state of mind, a particular brand, or a specific location.
The key constraints in this voice-based interpretation task are:
the absence of any predefined categories or inputs,
the need for the system to learn through self-discovery,
and for the output to be discrete rather than continuous.
To address this challenge, we developed a solution based on
pre-rankings and ensemble methods, and successfully demonstrated it on the task
of interpreting emotions expressed in spoken words, specifically without any
prior knowledge of distinct emotional categories. 
The system was evaluated using audio data from the IEMOCST dataset, and was
found to demonstrate comparable or better performance compared to prior methods.

We investigate two types of equations with both internal and boundary inclusions, focusing on their well-posedness within the context of weak solutions.  Furthermore, we examine the distinct characteristics and behaviors of the solutions in separate scenarios, one where temperatures and heat fluxes approach steady-state conditions and another where initial conditions play a crucial role.  This work seeks to expand the existing framework established in the theory of non-equilibrium thermodynamics.  As a related complement, we also consider a regularized problem with singularities to demonstrate the application of standard regularization techniques.  We hope this contribution will serve as a starting point for the development of more comprehensive models incorporating internal inclusions and active boundary processes.  The methods employed here rely on standard techniques from the existing literature, including the use of maximum principles, H\"older continuity, and the use of singular and regularized equations.  We also leverage the work of Antontsev, Shmarev, and Zhou on measure-type boundary conditions, and the work of Choe and Kohn on regularized equations with boundary inclusions.  We chose to present the results in this order, first focusing on the thermodynamic aspects and then the analytical aspects, in an effort to establish a connection between the theory of non-equilibrium interfaces and active boundary processes.  We believe this approach will facilitate a deeper understanding of the relationship between these two topics.  We have also included detailed proofs in the appendix to showcase the analytical methods and techniques used throughout this work.  As a result, our contribution falls within the established framework of non-equilibrium thermodynamics and analysis.  We plan to extend this work in future directions by developing more realistic models incorporating internal inclusions and active boundary processes.  The methods and techniques presented here will serve as a foundation for such extensions.  In the future, we hope to establish results for models with internal inclusions, boundary inclusions, and both internal and boundary inclusions, as well as results for models with multiple interfaces and active boundary processes.  We also plan to explore the connection between the analysis of thermodynamic equations and the analysis of phase field models.  We believe that by developing a comprehensive framework of non-equilibrium thermodynamics and analysis, we will make significant progress in the development of models and analysis of thermodynamic equations with internal inclusions and active boundary processes. This enhanced predictive capability enables distribution system operators to make more informed decisions, streamline operations, and prevent potential issues. Researchers achieved remarkable stabilization of electronic states through interaction with a highly energetic electromagnetic environment. An electron beam accelerated to 100 MeV was directed at a weak metal target within a synchrotron light source with extremely high energy density. As the electron beam interacted with the target, X-ray amplification occurred via stimulated Raman scattering. Our research centers on the goal of retrieving images based on their fashional characteristics, where we need to identify images that share a common fashion attribute despite potential variations in imagery and scene context. This goal is particularly challenging due to the scarcity and high cost of quality guides in this field. We have found that semi-automatically creating fake images with specific fashion attributes can serve as supplementary data to aid in this retrieval process. However, generating these fake images is a difficult problem, as we must ensure that they are indistinguishable from authentic images while also maintaining their desired fashion traits. To address this issue, we propose a novel technique for manipulating fashion images at a feature-level and a corresponding dataset with annotated fashion attributes. We have also developed a method of producing fake images and a retrieval method of selecting images based on these features. Our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, with experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness on a dataset of fashion images. To address well-posedness issues in inverse problems, researchers use minimization and regularization techniques to transform unconstrained non-regularized problems into constrained, regularized ones. Typically, these techniques rely on dual ascent in Hilbert spaces, but this approach is ill-suited for problems set in Banach spaces, which are more commonly encountered in practical applications. Therefore, a novel dual ascent method for constrained, regularized problems in Banach spaces is proposed, and its convergence is proven. This, in turn, establishes the convergence of an unconstrained, regularized dual ascent algorithm for problems set in any Banach space. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the proposed methods are applied to a range of theoretical and real-world inverse problems, including computational tomography, where the proposed methods outperform existing techniques by accurately reconstructing images in various settings. Furthermore, the proposed methods are shown to generalize and improve previously established methods, including the Lasso and Tikhonov methods. These methods are available on GitHub under the repository https://github.com/emanuele-vitali/dual-ascension-in-banach-spaces. Lastly, future research directions are identified, including the development of dual ascent methods for problems set in spaces with geometric constraints. These methods have the potential to address issues in machine learning, signal and image processing, machine learning, computational physics, and related fields. Evaluating the light field of a scene provides an in-depth understanding of its geometry and properties. Several methods have been proposed to estimate the depth of a scene from a light field, but many of these are inefficient and fail to account for occlusions. We introduce a novel approach called the Occlusion-Responsive Expense Creator (ORCE), which balances light field depth estimation accuracy with computational cost. By strategically reducing the cost for points near occlusions, ORCE achieves improved performance while remaining efficient. When integrated with the Quasi-Continuous Hard X-Ray Decoding method, ORCE achieves a significant 70% reduction in execution time with only a 2% decline in accuracy. Furthermore, ORORCE outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in both accuracy and efficiency. In our experiments, ORORCE achieved a 91.8% depth estimation accuracy on the standard "buddha" scene with a computational cost of $10^6$ multiplications, making it suitable for real-time applications on high-end mobile devices and computers. The proposed approach also scales well, enabling it to handle complex scenes with multiple occlusions. The method is further demonstrated by estimating the depth of a scene with a partially visible toy cat, as well as a scene with occlusions behind an opaque barrier, the "buddha with occlusion" scene. The approach outperformed all other methods in our tests, making it a significant advancement in light field depth assessment.
